findings.claim: `StoredEvent::is_verified()` has zero call sites in the entire workspace (verified by grep across .rs, .ts and .dart). The `verified` field it exposes is written `false` by every `StoredEvent::new` call site — 21 of them across buzz-relay, buzz-workflow and buzz-core tests — and `with_received_at` is the only constructor that can set it true. No delivery, fan-out, storage or bridge path ever consults it. The type therefore advertises a per-event 'verification status' (module doc, event.rs:1-4) that is never enforced, which invites a caller to assume verification is tracked when it is not.
findings.failure_scenario: A future caller constructs `StoredEvent::new(event, channel_id)` from an event that has not been through `verify_event` — for example `fan_out_pubsub_event` (crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/event.rs:292), which takes an event straight off the Redis pub/sub channel and never calls `verify_event` on it — and reasonably assumes the `verified` flag will stop unverified events at the send chokepoint. It will not: nothing reads the flag, so the event is serialised and delivered to subscribers regardless. Signature verification is in fact done only at the ingest boundary (ingest.rs:1844); anything entering via the pub/sub ingress inherits pod A's trust decision with no local check and no flag to notice its absence.

findings.claim: The module header asserts 'All constants are `u32` — NIP-01 specifies kind as an unsigned integer, and u32 covers the full range without truncation' (kind.rs:3-5), and `event_kind_u32` repeats it, but the underlying `nostr::Kind` is u16-backed and its `Deserialize` impl silently truncates: nostr-0.44.6/src/event/kind.rs `visit_u64` does `Ok(Self::Value::from(v as u16))`. A wire `"kind": 96158` is therefore accepted and folded to 30622 (`KIND_DM_VISIBILITY`); `"kind": 109736` folds to 44200. NIP-01 bounds kind to 0–65535, so a conforming relay would reject these outright.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker submits an event whose JSON says `"kind": 96158` while computing `id` and `sig` over the truncated value 30622. The relay's `verify_event` recomputes the id from the already-truncated `event.kind` and accepts the signature, so the event is admitted and every downstream kind check (`is_relay_only_kind`, `required_scope_for_kind`, the p-gates) sees 30622. Because the relay re-serialises the event before storage and fan-out (`serde_json::to_string(&stored_event.event)`, handlers/event.rs:448) the out-of-range value never leaves the relay, so no privilege is gained over simply sending 30622 directly — the practical effect is that an out-of-spec kind number is accepted instead of rejected, and that any external component (proxy, WAF, non-Rust pre-filter) inspecting the raw JSON kind will disagree with the relay about what kind the event is. Reported low confidence on exploitability: I found no path where the raw JSON text is retained or forwarded.

findings.claim: The mobile timeline resolves a kind:40003 edit event's target using the LAST `e` tag (`_lastETag`, line 586: it scans `for (var i = tags.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)`), while the relay authorizes the same event against the FIRST 64-hex `e` tag (crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs `validate_edit_ownership`, which does `event.tags.iter().find_map(...)`). Unlike kind:5/9005 deletions — which the relay explicitly caps at exactly one e/a tag (ingest.rs ~line 2338, `(e_count + a_count) != 1`) — there is no e-tag count restriction on kind:40003, and kind:40003 is in the relay's `skip_membership` list precisely because `validate_edit_ownership` is meant to be the sole authority. The client applies the edit with no author comparison at all: it overwrites both the target's `content` and its `tags` (line 473 `final effectiveTags = edit?.tags ?? event.tags;`, line 489 `content: edit?.content ?? event.content`) while keeping the original event's `pubkey`, so the forged text renders under the victim's name and avatar.
findings.failure_scenario: Mallory is a member of channel #eng. She posts an ordinary message M_a. She then publishes a kind:40003 event with tags [["h", "<eng-channel-id>"], ["e", "<M_a id>"], ["e", "<Alice's message id>"]] and content "approved, wire the funds to acct 12345". The relay's validate_edit_ownership reads the first e tag (M_a), sees author == actor, and accepts and fans out the event. Every mobile client that renders #eng runs formatTimeline over the channel window; `_lastETag` returns Alice's message id, so `edits[<Alice's message id>]` is set to Mallory's content and Mallory's tags. Alice's message row now displays Mallory's text, attributed to Alice's pubkey/display name/avatar, marked only with the generic 'edited' flag — and because `effectiveTags` comes from Mallory's event, Mallory also controls the p/mention tags rendered on Alice's message.

findings.claim: `parseNostrpairUri` accepts relay URLs from a scanned QR code after checking only that the scheme is `ws` or `wss` — no host validation whatsoever. The codebase already has a hardened validator for exactly this (`validateInviteRelayUri` in mobile/lib/shared/relay/relay_validation.dart, which rejects non-WSS outside debug, loopback, RFC1918, CGNAT, link-local, IPv4 literals in decimal/hex/leading-zero form, and non-global IPv6) and the invite deep-link path calls it (deep_link.dart line 170). The pairing QR path never does: `_pairNipAb` takes `qr.relays.first` (pairing_provider.dart line 178) and hands it straight to `PairingSocket`, which does `WebSocketChannel.connect(Uri.parse(_wsUrl))` (pairing_socket.dart line 63).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker prints or displays a QR encoding `nostrpair://<64-hex pubkey>?secret=<64-hex>&relay=ws%3A%2F%2F192.168.1.1%3A8080&v=1`. The user scans it on the pairing screen; pairing_page.dart line 54 passes the raw scanned string to `pair()`, which routes to `_pairNipAb`. The app opens a plaintext WebSocket to the victim's LAN gateway (or `ws://127.0.0.1:<port>` against another app on the device), sends a NIP-42 AUTH event signed with an ephemeral key, then a kind:24134 offer — turning the phone into an unauthenticated request source inside its own network segment, and doing the whole pairing handshake in cleartext where a local network attacker can read the session traffic. The SAS code still protects the key transfer itself, but the connection/probe happens before any user confirmation.

findings.claim: `_isPrivateHost`, the SSRF guard used by the legacy `buzz://` pairing path (`_validateRelayUrl`, line 654, called from `_parseLegacyInput` line 644 and from `_processPayload` line 461), is far weaker than the project's own `validateInviteRelayUri`. It only splits on '.' and requires exactly 4 decimal-parsable parts, so it misses: any non-dotted-quad literal (decimal `2130706433`, hex `0x7f000001`, octal/leading-zero `0177.0.0.1`, shortened `127.1`), all of 127.0.0.0/8 except the exact string `127.0.0.1` (the earlier check at line 665 is a literal string compare), 0.0.0.0/8, 100.64.0.0/10 CGNAT, and every IPv6 form other than the literal `::1`. `Uri.tryParse('http://$host')?.host` on line 672 does no normalization of these forms, but the platform resolver (getaddrinfo) does — so a host the check waves through resolves to loopback or LAN at connect time.
findings.failure_scenario: A user is handed a `buzz://<base64url payload>` pairing code (pasted into the pairing field or scanned as a QR — pairing_page.dart line 149 / line 54 both feed `pair()`). The payload decodes to {"relayUrl":"https://0177.0.0.1:8443","nsec":"..."} . `_validateRelayUrl` sees scheme https (OK in release), host is not the literal `localhost`/`127.0.0.1`/`::1`, and `_isPrivateHost` parses parts ['0177','0','0','1'] -> first octet 177, not private -> allowed. `_validateCredentials` then opens a WebSocket to `wss://0177.0.0.1:8443`, which the OS resolves to 127.0.0.1, i.e. a loopback service on the user's own device. The same trick with `https://2130706433` or `https://100.64.3.7` bypasses the check entirely because `parts.length != 4` returns false (not private).

findings.claim: When a tapped markdown link points at a relay media URL, `openDownloadedFileProvider` writes the response body to a temp file whose name — and therefore extension — comes from the markdown link *label*, then hands it to `OpenFilex.open`, which dispatches by extension. `_safeDownloadedFilename` (line 64) only strips path separators and control characters; it never constrains the extension or reconciles it with the server's Content-Type. The sibling image-download path in the same feature does exactly that reconciliation — `downloadedImageFilename` (mobile/lib/features/channels/message_actions.dart line 268) enforces an extension allowlist of avif/bmp/gif/heic/heif/jpe?g/png/webp and otherwise synthesizes one from Content-Type — so the safe pattern exists and was simply not applied here.
findings.failure_scenario: Mallory uploads arbitrary bytes to the relay as a generic attachment (media_upload.dart `uploadFile` sends them as application/octet-stream) and gets back a `https://<relay>/media/<hash>` URL. She posts the message `[Q3-financials.pdf.html](https://<relay>/media/<hash>)` in a channel. Bob taps it: `_buildLink` (line 339) sees an http(s) scheme, `auth.isRelayMediaUrl(url)` returns true because the host matches the relay and the path starts with /media/, so `openDownloadedFileProvider` runs with `filename = 'Q3-financials.pdf.html'`. The bytes land in the temp dir as `<micros>-Q3-financials.pdf.html` and `OpenFilex.open` launches the system HTML handler on attacker-controlled markup, from a same-app content:// URI, while the user believed they were opening a PDF from a trusted relay host. Any extension works (.html, .svg, .xml, .url); the label and the actual bytes need have no relationship.

findings.claim: `shouldNotifyForEvent` evaluates the sender-controlled `broadcast` tag and `p` tags BEFORE it consults the user's mute sets. `mutedChannelIds` is only checked at line 35 and `mutedRootIds` only at line 42, both after two unconditional `return true` paths driven purely by attacker-chosen tags. `broadcast` is not a privileged marker — desktop/src/features/messages/lib/threading.ts treats `["broadcast","1"]` as an ordinary client-set flag meaning 'post this reply to the channel timeline', and the relay's kind mapping puts kind:9/40002 under the plain MessagesWrite scope. So the user's mute decision is computed but not enforced against any sender who sets the tag.
findings.failure_scenario: Bob mutes the noisy #random channel (its id goes into `_mutedChannelIds()`, channels_provider.dart line 285) or mutes a specific thread root. Mallory posts a kind:9 message in #random carrying the tag ["broadcast","1"]. `shouldNotifyForEvent` hits the broadcast loop at line 19-23 and returns true before reaching the `mutedChannelIds.contains(eventChannelId)` guard, so the channel is re-surfaced with an unread/high-priority badge and its `lastMessageAt` is bumped. Mallory can repeat this indefinitely; the mute control is effectively opt-out-able by the sender.

findings.claim: `fetchHistory` sends a REQ carrying a `limit` (NostrFilter.limit, default 100, serialized at nostr_models.dart line 239) but the client never enforces that limit on what actually arrives: `_handleEvent` appends every EVENT frame for a history subscription into an unbounded `List<NostrEvent>` and only stops at EOSE or the 8-second timeout. There is no cap on event count, no cap on cumulative bytes, and `NostrEvent.fromJson` imposes no bound on `tags` or `content` size. The same unbounded-accumulation shape exists on the live path (`_eventBuffer`, line 466, drained only every 16 ms).
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious or compromised relay (or a relay operator who wants to brick a specific client) answers any REQ — e.g. the channel history fetch issued on opening a channel — with a continuous stream of oversized EVENT frames and never sends EOSE. For 8 seconds the client parses each frame into a NostrEvent and pushes it onto `historySub.events` with no ceiling; on a phone this is a straightforward OOM kill of the app, and it repeats on every reconnect because the failure happens before any timeout-driven CLOSE is sent. The client's own stated bound (`limit`) is transmitted to the peer being defended against and never re-checked locally.

findings.claim: `MediaImageProvider._loadAsync` fetches arbitrary attacker-supplied URLs with `client.get(uri, ...)` and materializes the entire response into memory via `response.bodyBytes` before decoding, with no Content-Length check, no streaming cap and no request timeout. The URLs come straight out of untrusted event data: every markdown image in a message (`MessageContent._buildMedia` -> `MediaImage(url: imageUrl)`, message_content.dart line 436), every `imeta` poster URL, every kind:0 `picture` avatar (ProfileData.avatarUrl, nostr_models.dart line 282), and every custom-emoji URL. The existing `_cooldownUntil` throttle only limits retry *frequency* after a failure; it does nothing about the size of a successful response.
findings.failure_scenario: Mallory posts `![x](https://evil.example/10gb.bin)` in a channel, or sets her kind:0 `picture` field to that URL. Every mobile client that scrolls the message (or renders her avatar anywhere — member list, mention chip, DM row) issues an unbounded GET; the server streams multi-gigabyte content and `response.bodyBytes` accumulates all of it in the Dart heap before any decode limit applies, killing the app on memory pressure. Because it is an avatar, the fetch re-triggers on many unrelated screens rather than requiring the victim to open a specific message.

findings.claim: The `<application>` element declares no `android:allowBackup="false"`, no `android:dataExtractionRules` and no `android:fullBackupContent`. Android's default is `allowBackup="true"`, so the app's private data directory — which holds the flutter_secure_storage backing store used by CommunityStorage for `buzz_communities` (the JSON list of communities including each community's `nsec`, mobile/lib/shared/community/community_storage.dart lines 8 and 107-110) and the SharedPreferences used for read-state and theme — is enrolled in Android Auto Backup / device-to-device transfer. flutter_secure_storage's own guidance is to disable backup for exactly this reason. Note the app also targets no `networkSecurityConfig`; cleartext is blocked only by the targetSdk default.
findings.failure_scenario: The user's device data is transferred or restored (Google Auto Backup to Drive, or a device-to-device migration). The encrypted credential blob for every paired community leaves the device without the user ever being prompted about key material specifically. On the restore side, the Keystore-held AES key does not travel, so the restored blob is undecryptable — the practical outcome is either an unexplained loss of all community credentials after a restore, or, where the storage plugin falls back to a non-Keystore path, off-device exposure of the blob. I could not trace this to a remote attacker-controlled entry point; it is a platform-hardening gap, reported at correspondingly low confidence in terms of exploitability.

findings.claim: lastSeenCreatedAt is advanced when an event is merely buffered (before delivery), but _handleDisconnected clears _eventBuffer without rolling lastSeenCreatedAt back; the reconnect replay then uses since = lastSeenCreatedAt - 5s, so buffered-but-undelivered events older than that are permanently lost to the live subscription.
findings.failure_scenario: Flaky network: after a reconnect, _replayLiveSubscriptions (line 416) delivers a burst covering the whole disconnect gap (possibly minutes of messages). _handleEvent buffers them and advances liveSub.lastSeenCreatedAt to the newest event's timestamp (lines 462-465) while they sit in _eventBuffer awaiting the 16ms flush timer. The connection drops again inside that window -> _handleDisconnected runs _eventBuffer.clear() (line 387) so onEvent never fires for any of them, yet lastSeenCreatedAt still points at the newest. The next replay sends since = newest-5s, so every discarded event older than 5s before the newest is never redelivered. Note _handleEose only flushes for subscriptions with a readyCompleter (initial subscribe), not reconnect replays. User sees messages silently missing from open channel timelines until a full history refetch.

findings.claim: The open-channel live subscription filters with since = local wall-clock now with zero skew allowance, so any incoming message whose sender-signed created_at is even one second behind the local clock is excluded by the relay's filter and never delivered live; with a fast local clock, live delivery for the open channel silently fails entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: _init() (line 74) subscribes with since: _currentUnixSeconds() (line 88, local DateTime.now()), then fetches history. A peer whose device clock is 30s behind (common on Android without NTT sync) sends a message: its created_at is 30s older than the mobile client's since bound, the relay's NIP-01 filter check rejects it for this subscription, and the earlier history fetch already completed - the message appears only after the user leaves and re-enters the channel. The codebase itself acknowledges skew elsewhere (relay_session's _reconnectReplaySkewSeconds = 5, and channels_provider's list subscription uses limit:0 with no since), making this filter the odd one out. channel_window.dart line 333 additionally drops live rows older than the loaded window bottom, so even a since fix needs care.

findings.claim: The MediaMuxer remux copies track formats via addTrack(format) but never calls muxer.setOrientationHint() with the source's rotation, and MediaMuxer does not honor KEY_ROTATION from addTrack; portrait videos recorded with rotation metadata are written without it and upload sideways.

The uploaded MP4 plays rotated 90 degrees for every recipient on desktop and mobile. iOS is unaffected (AVAssetExportSession passthrough preserves the transform), making it an Android-only rendering divergence.

findings.claim: _publish silently drops a scheduled publish when another publish is in flight (if (_isPublishing) return;) without rescheduling, and dispose() only flushes when a debounce timer is still pending, so read-state advances made during a slow in-flight publish are never synced to the relay until some unrelated later markContextRead.

User reads channel A (publish starts), then reads channel B; the 5s debounce fires during the in-flight publish, _publish() returns immediately at line 388 with the timer already consumed (_debounceTimer = null in _schedulePublish's callback, line 376). Channel B's advance sits only in _effectiveState. User backgrounds/kills the app: dispose() sees _debounceTimer == null -> hadPendingPublish false -> no flush (lines 157-165). Desktop and other devices keep showing channel B as unread; the state resyncs only after the user marks something else read on mobile.

findings.claim: Relay frames are consumed with unchecked casts (data[0] as String here; data[1] as String / data[2] as bool in _handleOk; data[2] as Map and per-element tag casts in relay_session._handleEvent + NostrEvent.fromJson), so a single structurally malformed frame from the relay throws an uncaught TypeError inside the WebSocket onData callback instead of being dropped like malformed JSON is.

If it happens during NIP-42 auth, the AUTH challenge is lost and the connection stalls until the 8s auth timeout. Contrast: malformed JSON at line 164-168 is deliberately caught and ignored, showing the intended contract that bad frames must not throw.

findings.claim: A stream error during NIP-42 auth triggers _onDisconnected twice for the same connection generation: once from the onError handler and once from connect()'s catch block after the auth completer rejects, so RelaySessionNotifier._handleDisconnected runs twice, double-incrementing reconnectAttempt and re-running _cancelAllHistory/_scheduleReconnect.

The completer rejection resumes connect()'s await, whose catch runs await disconnect(); _onDisconnected(e) (second call, lines 112-116). relay_session._handleDisconnected has only a generation guard (line 384), which both calls pass, so the reconnect state machine processes one disconnect as two: the UI-visible reconnectAttempt counter inflates by 2 per failure and the backoff timer is cancelled and recreated. No message loss, but the reconnect state/telemetry is wrong.

findings.claim: The kind:39002 membership pagination advances with until = min(created_at) - 1, which skips any remaining membership events sharing the boundary second when a 500-event page cuts mid-timestamp, so some joined channels can be silently absent from the channel list.

The relay returns 500 rows ending mid-second; the next query uses until = boundary - 1, permanently excluding the unreturned events at that second. Those channels never enter channelIds (line 145) and are invisible in the app until some later event changes their membership timestamp. Requires large membership plus timestamp collisions at the cut, hence low.

The community switcher UI shows only the new community; previously joined communities reappear only after the provider is invalidated (e.g. app restart or removeCommunity path). findings.claim: Any input that does not start with `nostrpair://` silently falls back to the legacy pairing flow, which base64-decodes an attacker-supplied JSON blob and imports its `nsec` + `relayUrl` as the active identity with no SAS, no transcript-hash check, no signature check and no confirmation dialog — a protocol downgrade the attacker chooses. The modern NIP-AB path (`_pairNipAb`) requires a 6-digit SAS the user must visually match; the legacy path requires nothing. The QR scanner feeds raw barcode text straight in: PairingPage.handleScannerResult -> `pair(code)` (pairing_provider.dart:91) -> `_pairLegacy` (line 103) -> `_parseLegacyInput` (line 625) -> `_validateCredentials` (line 569) -> `authenticateWithCommunity` (line 574), which writes the attacker's nsec to secure storage and switches the app to the attacker's relay. Grepping the whole repo shows no component still produces this legacy format (desktop's `desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/pairing.rs` and `crates/buzz-core/src/pairing/qr.rs` emit only `nostrpair://`), so this is a dead-but-live credential-injection path.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker prints/posts a QR whose payload is base64url of {"relayUrl":"https://evil.example","pubkey":"<attacker>","nsec":"nsec1<attacker>"} captioned "scan to join our Buzz community". Victim taps Scan on the unauthenticated PairingPage (lib/app.dart:104 makes PairingPage the landing screen) or on Add Community. `_firstScannedValue` (pairing_qr_scanner.dart:82) returns the raw string, `pair()` routes it to `_pairLegacy`, and the app authenticates as the attacker-controlled identity against the attacker's relay. Every message, media upload and NIP-42 AUTH the victim then performs is signed with a key the attacker also holds and is delivered to the attacker's relay; the attacker can read everything the victim writes and impersonate the victim to anyone who trusts that key. The victim sees a normal "connected" UI, never a SAS prompt.

findings.claim: `_validateRelayUrl`/`_isPrivateHost` is a second, much weaker copy of the SSRF guard that already exists in `lib/shared/relay/relay_validation.dart`. `_isPrivateHost` returns false for anything that is not exactly four dotted-decimal parts, so it misses: shortened IPv4 (`127.1`), integer/hex IPv4 (`2130706433`, `0x7f000001`), leading-zero octets, all IPv6 including unique-local (`fd00::/8`) and IPv4-mapped (`[::ffff:127.0.0.1]`), CGNAT `100.64.0.0/10`, benchmark `198.18.0.0/15`, and `0.0.0.0/8`. Only the literal strings `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `::1` are special-cased above it (lines 665-670). `relay_validation.validateInviteRelayUri` correctly rejects all of these (relay_validation.dart:38-67, 145-164), so the pairing path is strictly weaker than the invite path for the same class of untrusted URL.
findings.failure_scenario: A hostile pairing QR (either the legacy blob or a NIP-AB `payload`, both of which reach `_validateRelayUrl` at lines 461 and 644) carries relayUrl `https://127.1/` or `https://[fd00::1]/`. Validation passes, the community is stored, and RelaySessionNotifier then opens `wss://127.1/` (relay_provider.dart:55-59) and completes a NIP-42 AUTH handshake against it — signing a kind:22242 event with the user's key and directing all traffic to a loopback or link-local service on the victim's device/LAN, which is exactly what this check exists to prevent.

findings.claim: The user's Nostr private key (nsec) is persisted through `const FlutterSecureStorage()` with no platform options at all. flutter_secure_storage 10.x defaults iOS keychain accessibility to `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked` (not `...ThisDeviceOnly`), which means the item is included in encrypted device backups and restorable onto a different device; and the Android manifest declares no `android:allowBackup="false"`, no `android:dataExtractionRules` and no `android:fullBackupContent`, so the app's data is backup/transfer-eligible by default. Nothing in the app opts out: `IOSOptions`/`AndroidOptions` appear nowhere in the slice. The key is the whole identity (relay_provider.dart:112-115 derives the pubkey from it, relay_socket.dart:196 signs NIP-42 AUTH with it, media_auth.dart:102 and relay_session.dart:676 sign HTTP auth with it), and NIP-AB itself warns that after transfer "the transferred key's security depends entirely on the receiving device's storage".
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who obtains an encrypted iTunes/Finder backup of the victim's iPhone (or a Google/D2D transfer image on Android) restores it to a device they control. Because the keychain item was not created with a `ThisDeviceOnly` accessibility class, it is carried into the restore and the attacker's device now holds the victim's nsec — full, non-revocable impersonation on the victim's relay, since Nostr has no key-revocation mechanism.

findings.claim: `_cleanup()` tears down the socket and the consent flags but never clears the session's key material: `_ephemeralPrivkey`, `_ephemeralPubkey`, `_sessionSecret`, `_sasInput`, `_sessionId`, `_conversationKey` and `_sourcePubkey` (declared at lines 157-163) all survive. `PairingNotifier` is a root-scope `NotifierProvider` (line 697) that is never auto-disposed, so the ephemeral private key, the QR session secret and the NIP-44 conversation key of every pairing the user has ever run stay live in the process heap for the app's lifetime. NIP-AB §Step 5 states: "Implementations MUST zero the ephemeral private keys, session secret, and any decrypted payload plaintext from memory before freeing" — only `_pendingPayload` is nulled here.
findings.failure_scenario: After a successful pairing the app keeps running for days. Anything that captures process memory — an OS crash dump, a debugger on a jailbroken/rooted device, a memory-scraping exploit in another loaded library — recovers `_sessionSecret` and `_ephemeralPrivkey`, which together with relay-retained kind:24134 ciphertext (relays MAY retain these for a TTL) let the attacker recompute the conversation key and decrypt the transferred payload, i.e. the victim's nsec. Marked low because it requires local memory access; the deviation from the spec's MUST is unambiguous.

findings.claim: `_unpad` validates only that the declared length fits inside the buffer (`2 + len > padded.length`); it never checks that the buffer is exactly the canonical padded size, i.e. `padded.length == 2 + calcPaddedLen(len)`, which NIP-44 v2 requires. `_calcPaddedLen` exists (line 93) but is used only by `_pad` on the encrypt side. Separately, `nip44Decrypt` enforces a 97-byte floor (line 63) but no upper bound, whereas NIP-AB §Event Validation step 5 requires discarding kind:24134 events whose content is outside 132–87472 base64 characters, and `_handlePairingEvent` (pairing_provider.dart:344-348) performs no such length check before calling in.
findings.failure_scenario: Two peers sharing a conversation key are no longer guaranteed a unique wire encoding for a given plaintext: a party that holds the key can append arbitrary trailing bytes inside the padded region and produce a second, differently-sized ciphertext that decrypts to the identical plaintext and passes the MAC, defeating any dedupe or replay logic that keys on the ciphertext. In the pairing path the missing size ceiling additionally lets a relay push a multi-megabyte `content` string that is base64-decoded, HKDF-expanded and ChaCha20-processed before the HMAC check rejects it. Low confidence on real-world impact: forging the MAC without the conversation key is not possible, so this is primarily a spec-conformance and DoS-surface defect rather than a decryption break.

findings.claim: When a message link points at relay-hosted media, the app downloads the bytes and hands the file to the OS via `OpenFilex.open`, naming it from the markdown link *text* rather than from anything about the actual content. `_safeDownloadedFilename` (line 64) strips path separators and control characters but deliberately preserves the extension, and no `Content-Type` check is performed. Both halves are attacker-controlled: any community member can PUT arbitrary bytes to the relay's Blossom media endpoint (media_upload.dart:402-433) and then post `[quarterly.pdf](https://relay/media/<hash>)`, so the extension that selects the platform handler is decoupled from the bytes.

A victim taps it; message_content.dart:346-356 recognises it as a relay media URL, downloads it with the victim's Blossom auth header, writes it to the temp directory as `<ts>-minutes.html`, and OpenFilex hands it to the system viewer, which renders attacker HTML/JS in whatever handler the OS picks for that extension. The user's only signal that the file is not what it claims is the link text the attacker wrote.

The `buzz` scheme is registered as an exported, BROWSABLE intent filter (android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:42-47) and as a CFBundleURLScheme on iOS (Info.plist:32-35), so any installed app or any web page the user visits can trigger it.

findings.claim: A live subscription's high-water mark `lastSeenCreatedAt` is advanced to the raw attacker-chosen `event.created_at` with no clamp to the current time, and that value later becomes the `since` floor for the reconnect-replay REQ — so one future-dated event silently suppresses all real messages delivered after a reconnect.
findings.failure_scenario: A channel member (anyone the relay lets publish a CHANNEL_EVENT_KINDS event with `#h`=<channel>) posts a single event with `created_at` set far in the future (e.g. year 2100). It matches the victim's live channel subscription filter, so RelayClient.handleEvent -> prepareSubscriptionEvent runs and sets `lastSeenCreatedAt = Math.max(prev, 4102444800)`. Live delivery is unaffected (live mode always returns true), so nothing looks wrong. On the next WebSocket drop/reconnect (routine on mobile/VPN), replayLiveSubscriptions computes `replaySince = lastSeenCreatedAt - 5` (relayReconnectReplay.ts:170-176) and buildReconnectReplayFilter sets the replay REQ `since` to that future timestamp. The relay returns no events in the gap between the reconnect and the year 2100, and the paging path's `while (pageUntil >= since)` (relayReconnectReplay.ts:96) never runs because now < since — so every message the victim missed during the drop, plus everything posted afterward until real time reaches the poisoned timestamp, is silently dropped from that channel with no error surfaced.

findings.claim: The ancestor-backfill dedupe set is capped by *evicting* its oldest entries, which destroys the very memory that prevents re-fetching. Once a channel session accumulates more than 500 distinct missing-ancestor ids (2 per attacker message: `reply` + `root`), every subsequent run of the effect re-requests the evicted ids, and the effect re-runs on every change to `resolvedMessages` — i.e. on every live event in the channel. Attacker-chosen `e` tags therefore drive an unbounded, repeating stream of `getEventById` relay queries from the victim's client.
findings.failure_scenario: Mallory, a member of channel X, posts 260 ordinary messages, each carrying `["e", <random-64-hex>, "", "reply"]` and `["e", <another-random-64-hex>, "", "root"]` pointing at ids that do not exist (or exist in a different channel). Alice opens channel X. `useLoadMissingAncestors` collects ~520 missing ancestor ids (line 43-53), inserts them into `requestedAncestorIdsRef` (line 60-62), then trims the set back to 500 by deleting the first ~20 (lines 65-76), and fires ~520 `getEventById` calls (line 80-100). Every fetch either throws or is discarded by the channel-id check at line 87, so none of those ids ever enters `knownEvents`. The next time any live event lands in the channel, `resolvedMessages` gets a new identity, the effect re-runs, and the ~20 evicted ids are missing again — re-added, re-evicted, re-fetched. Scaling Mallory's message count so that the evicted `excess` is in the hundreds turns each incoming channel message into hundreds of relay round-trips from Alice's client, wedging her UI and amplifying load on the relay. The messages persist in the channel, so the loop restarts on every reopen.

findings.claim: A relay event's `created_at` is taken raw as the channel's "latest observed" timestamp and is later folded into the published NIP-RS read marker with `Math.max` and no upper clamp against wall-clock time (`resolveChannelReadMarker`, line 114). Because `ReadStateManager.advanceContext` is strictly monotonic (readStateManager.ts:381 `if (unixTimestamp <= current) ... return`), a single far-future timestamp permanently pins the marker, and the marker is encrypted, published, and synced to all of the user's devices. LOW confidence on exploitability: I found a ±900s drift guard in crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs (`MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS`), so a conforming relay blocks the input. This is a defense-in-depth gap — the client trusts the relay's clock check with no clamp of its own, and any relay bug, misconfigured/older relay, or clock-skewed deployment silently and irreversibly silences a channel.
findings.failure_scenario: A member (or a relay deployment whose drift guard is bypassed/disabled/skewed) publishes one channel message with `created_at = 4102444800` (year 2100). Alice's client records it via `handleChannelMessage` (line 421-423) into `latestByChannelRef`. The next time Alice marks the channel read — pressing Esc, clicking the sidebar, or just opening it (ChannelScreen.tsx:214, useMarkAsReadShortcuts.ts:43) — `resolveChannelReadMarker` returns `Math.max(callerUnix, 4102444800)` and `markContextRead(channelId, 4102444800)` runs. From then on every genuine message fails `event.created_at > readAt` (line 675) and the channel is permanently marked read on every device, with no UI to lower the marker. There is no clamp such as `Math.min(ts, now + tolerance)` anywhere on the client path.

findings.claim: get_thread_replies_on silently skips rows that fail event reconstruction, but unlike get_channel_window it has no limit+1 has_more probe — clients derive EOF from row count (documented in lib.rs:2690-2691: 'an under-limit page is a candidate terminal page — the client treats it as EOF'), so a single unreconstructable reply row permanently truncates thread pagination at that page.

The same file already documents and fixes this exact hazard for channel windows (ChannelWindow.has_more, thread.rs:73-75: 'callers must not re-derive exhaustion from row counts'), but the thread-replies path was left on count-based EOF.

findings.claim: StoredEvent carries a `verified` flag with a public accessor that has zero call sites anywhere in the workspace, while the constructor used by every relay live-fan-out site hardcodes it to false — a verification signal nothing consults.
findings.failure_scenario: A grep for `is_verified()` across the whole repo returns only its definition here; no crate ever branches on it. Meanwhile StoredEvent::new (event.rs:23) hardcodes `verified: false` and is the constructor used at every relay live-delivery site (crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/event.rs:292, :864, :892, :1081, :2117, crates/buzz-relay/src/api/bridge.rs:2864, crates/buzz-relay/src/audio/handler.rs:1306), whereas with_received_at(..., true) is what the DB read path uses (crates/buzz-db/src/lib.rs:4567, :4741, :4978). The two constructors therefore disagree about the meaning of the field for the same event. The failure is latent rather than active: a future reviewer or a new delivery surface that adds `if stored.is_verified() { deliver }` would silently drop every live-fan-out event, and one that adds `if !stored.is_verified() { verify() }` would re-verify DB rows while trusting live ones. Signature safety today rests entirely on ingest.rs:1843 spawn_blocking(verify_event) and this field contributes nothing to it.

findings.claim: UpdateKind::classify hardcodes the 40-character SHA-1 zero OID, so in a SHA-256 repository a ref deletion (64-character zero new_oid) is classified NonFastForward instead of Delete and a `no-delete` protection rule never fires.
findings.failure_scenario: Repository OIDs are not assumed to be SHA-1 elsewhere in the codebase: crates/buzz-relay/src/api/git/manifest_event.rs:291 has an explicit test named accepts_sha1_and_sha256_oids pinning that a 64-hex OID is accepted. The pre-receive hook shares the same assumption (crates/buzz-relay/src/api/git/hook.rs:41 defines ZERO as 40 zeros, and only sets IS_ANCESTOR when both OIDs differ from that literal). In a SHA-256 repo a delete arrives as old=<64 hex>, new=<64 zeros>: the hook's `[ "$new_oid" != "$ZERO" ]` guard is true so it runs merge-base against a nonexistent object and reports is_ancestor=false, and classify then returns NonFastForward. evaluate_ref_update (git_perms.rs:530) checks `effective.no_force_push && update.kind == UpdateKind::NonFastForward` and `effective.no_delete && update.kind == UpdateKind::Delete`. So for a rule ["buzz-protect","refs/heads/main","no-delete"] with no `no-force-push`, an Admin (who already satisfies default_min_role for NonFastForward) deletes the protected branch: the no_delete branch is never reached. The module docs state protection rules 'apply to everyone (including the owner)', so this is a protection bypass, not just a misclassification. Low confidence because I did not confirm the deployment actually provisions SHA-256 repositories — if only SHA-1 repos exist, the bug is unreachable.

findings.claim: decode_qr parses the pairing URI's protocol version with `.ok()`, silently discarding a parse failure and falling back to version 1, so a URI that declares an unsupported version non-numerically is accepted as v1 instead of rejected; duplicate query parameters are also last-wins.
findings.failure_scenario: The version check at qr.rs:155-160 rejects `version != 1`, but only after `let version = version.unwrap_or(1)`. Because line 148 stores `value.parse::<u32>().ok()`, any unparseable value yields None and therefore the default. `nostrpair://<pk>?secret=<hex>&relay=wss%3A%2F%2Fr&v=2x` is accepted and processed as a v1 session, defeating the explicit rejection the module's own reject_unsupported_version test pins. The same loop is last-wins for every key, so `...&v=2&v=` also downgrades to v1, and `...&secret=<attacker>&secret=<real>` lets a crafted URI carry two secrets where a naive scanner UI might display one and the parser use the other. The practical exposure is bounded — the scanning device is the party choosing to trust the QR, and a v2 protocol does not exist yet — so this is a forward-compatibility / strictness defect rather than a present break. It matters because this URI is the sole bootstrap for a session that transports an nsec (PayloadType::Nsec in pairing/types.rs:66), so silently reinterpreting a future version under v1 semantics is exactly the downgrade the version field exists to prevent.

findings.claim: A live subscription's reconnect watermark `lastSeenCreatedAt` is set from the raw, unvalidated `created_at` of every inbound relay EVENT, so one event with a far-future timestamp permanently poisons the watermark and every subsequent reconnect replays with a `since` in the future — silently dropping all missed messages for that subscription for the rest of the session.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker path: (1) any community member (or the relay itself) publishes a kind:9/kind:11 event into channel X with `created_at = 4102444800` (year 2100). The relay's ingest path does not bound future timestamps — crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/command_executor.rs:121-125 only rejects timestamps that `chrono::DateTime::from_timestamp` cannot represent — so the event is stored and fanned out. (2) The victim's client receives it: relayClientSession.ts:783 matches the `EVENT` frame and calls `this.handleEvent(rest[0], rest[1] as RelayEvent)` with zero shape or range validation. (3) relayClientSession.ts:859 calls `prepareSubscriptionEvent(subscription, event)`. (4) relayClosedRecovery.ts:141-144 executes `subscription.lastSeenCreatedAt = Math.max(lastSeenCreatedAt ?? 0, event.created_at)` → the watermark becomes 4102444800 and can never be lowered (Math.max). (5) On the next socket drop, relayClientSession.ts:934 calls `replayLiveSubscriptions`, which at relayReconnectReplay.ts:170-176 computes `replaySince = max(0, 4102444800 - 5)` and at relayReconnectReplay.ts:61 builds the REQ filter with `since: Math.max(filter.since, since)`. (6) The REQ sent at relayReconnectReplay.ts:213-219 asks the relay for events newer than the year 2100, so the relay returns nothing. The victim's channel silently stops backfilling on every reconnect from then on — no error, no UI indication, and the paged-replay branch (`replayReconnectHistoryPages`, since > until) exits immediately too. One attacker message permanently breaks reconnect recovery for every client subscribed to that channel.

findings.claim: The community custom-emoji palette resolves shortcode collisions purely by comparing attacker-chosen `event.created_at` values with no upper bound, so any member can publish a kind:30030 set with a far-future timestamp and permanently take over every shortcode in the community — no honest member can ever outbid the forged timestamp.

The relay does not bound future `created_at` on ingest and performs no validation of the emoji tag's URL. (2) Every client calls `listCustomEmoji()` → `fetchCommunityEmojiEvents()` (customEmoji.ts:137-146, `limit: 500` across all members) → `unionCustomEmoji(events)`. Impact: community-wide emoji substitution (content spoofing) plus an unrevokable per-render beacon to an attacker-controlled host that leaks each viewer's IP and User-Agent.

findings.claim: A relay-controlled CLOSED message string decides whether a live subscription is retried or permanently deleted, so a single crafted CLOSED frame silently and irrecoverably removes a channel's live subscription for the rest of the session with no user-visible signal.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker path: the relay answers a live REQ with `["CLOSED", "live-<uuid>", "auth-required: re-auth"]` (the relay knows the subId because the client sent it). (1) relayClientSession.ts:806-818 routes this to `handleRelayClosed`. (2) `recoverLiveSubscriptionFromClosed` calls `classifyRelayClosed(message)` (relayClosedRecovery.ts:79), which at relayClosedPolicy.ts:22-34 returns `"terminal"` for any message beginning with `restricted:`, `auth-required:`, `blocked:`, `invalid:`, `pow:`, `duplicate:`, or `unsupported:` — all attacker-chosen prefixes. (3) relayClosedRecovery.ts:81-86 then does `subscriptions.delete(subId); return;` with no callback to the subscriber, no rejection, and no connection-state change. findings.claim: verify_auth_tag only syntax-checks the NIP-OA `conditions` string and never evaluates its clauses, and it takes no event to evaluate them against — so the relay's membership paths, which are its main consumers, grant access on an attestation whose `created_at<T` lifetime bound has already passed. docs/nips/NIP-OA.md states "Verifiers MUST evaluate every clause" and "Owners SHOULD bound authorization lifetime with a `created_at<...` clause when revocation latency matters"; the SDK exposes no clause-evaluation helper, so buzz-cli hand-rolls one (buzz-cli/src/commands/users.rs:196 `auth_conditions_apply`) while the relay does not.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner who is a relay member issues an agent an auth tag with conditions `created_at<1700000000`, intending it to expire, then stops trusting the agent. The agent (or anyone who copies the tag off a public event — the tag is a reusable capability by design, NIP-OA.md line 16) connects to a closed relay and sends a kind:22242 AUTH event carrying that tag. handlers/auth.rs:78 extracts it, handlers/auth.rs:221 passes it to enforce_relay_membership, which reaches api/mod.rs:86 `verify_auth_tag(tag_json, &agent_pubkey)`. That call returns Ok(owner_pubkey) at nip_oa.rs:235 because the Schnorr signature is valid; nothing compares the expired `created_at<` bound against anything, and the AUTH event's own kind (22242) is never checked against a `kind=` clause either. api/mod.rs:96 then finds the owner is a relay member and returns ViaOwner, so the revoked agent authenticates. The same unevaluated path is used by the HTTP surface (api/mod.rs:160 extract_nip_oa_owner) and by the ban cascade in handlers/auth.rs:137.

findings.claim: count_events_on silently ignores EventQuery::shared_gated_reader. The SELECT builder query_events_on applies the shared-gate visibility clause at event.rs:538-550 (`AND (kind NOT IN (SHARED_GATED_KINDS) OR pubkey = $reader OR tags @> '[["shared","true"]]')`), but the COUNT builder ends at line 764 without ever reading that field — even though callers set it on the very struct they hand to the count path (buzz-relay/src/handlers/count.rs:163 and :235, buzz-relay/src/api/bridge.rs:1547). The only thing preventing a private-event count leak is a separate `&& !needs_shared_gate_filtering` term in the caller's if-condition; the field itself is a no-op, which is exactly the shape the route_proof module warns about at lib.rs:330 ("if the two ever drift ... the routed COUNT seam is unsound").
findings.failure_scenario: A reader issues a NIP-45 COUNT for a shared-gated kind (SHARED_GATED_KINDS, e.g. 30175/30178) authored by another user. count.rs:163 sets query.shared_gated_reader = Some(reader) and the code today falls into the query+post-filter branch only because of the extra `!needs_shared_gate_filtering` guard on the same condition. If that guard is dropped, reordered, or a new caller (or the bridge's future count seam) constructs the same EventQuery and calls count_events/count_events_routed directly, count_events_on emits SQL with no visibility predicate and returns the count of other users' non-shared private events. Combined with attacker-chosen `authors`, `since`, and `until` on the same filter, the counts binary-search the existence and timing of private items the SELECT path would never return.

findings.claim: get_accessible_channel_ids returns every open channel in the community with no LIMIT and no cap, unlike its sibling get_accessible_channels which caps the same result set at LIMIT 1000 (channel.rs:973-975). The unbounded Vec<Uuid> is then written straight into EventQuery::channel_ids (buzz-relay/src/handlers/req.rs:1008, count.rs:232, api/bridge.rs:1543), and event.rs:418-425 turns it into one bind parameter per channel in an `IN (...)` list on every historical REQ/COUNT page. No per-community channel quota exists anywhere in the workspace (grep for max_channels/channel_limit/MAX_CHANNELS returns nothing).
findings.failure_scenario: A relay member in community X creates open channels in a loop via kind:40001/9007 (channel creation is not quota-limited). At N open channels, every subsequent REQ from every member of X — including the attacker's victims — resolves an N-element Uuid vector at channel.rs:751, caches a copy per (community, pubkey) in state.rs:1105, and issues a query with N bind parameters plus an N-element IN list. Past ~10,900 channels the events query is already carrying more binds than most planners handle well, and past 65,535 total parameters the Postgres extended-protocol limit is hit and every historical read in that community fails with a bind error rather than a graceful cap. Because the cap is present on the sibling function, the omission is a per-tenant self-DoS reachable by any member.

findings.claim: mention_tags caps the number of mentions and lowercases them but never validates that each entry is a 64-character hex pubkey, so build_message (line 232), build_forum_post (286) and build_forum_comment (302) will sign arbitrary caller-supplied strings into `p` tags. Every other p-tag emitter in the same file validates: build_dm_open uses check_pubkey_hex (1552), build_dm_add_member uses check_pubkey_hex (1560), build_contact_list rejects anything not exactly 64 hex chars (777-782), and build_agent_observer_frame uses check_pubkey_hex (262-263).
findings.failure_scenario: An agent/MCP caller (or any code path that forwards a user-supplied mention list) calls build_message(channel, text, None, &["<4KiB of arbitrary text>", "NOT-A-PUBKEY"], false, &[]). The builder emits ["p","<4kib of arbitrary text>"] and the caller signs it, so the malformed p-tag is now inside a signature-protected event that the relay stores verbatim and fans out to every subscriber. Buzz's own ingest indexer defends itself — insert_mentions at lib.rs:132 drops p-tags that are not 64 hex chars — but nothing else does: the tag ships to third-party Nostr clients that treat p-tag[1] as a pubkey, and 50 such tags let a single 64KiB-content message carry ~200KiB of unvalidated attacker text in a field the builder's own contract documents as "pubkey hex strings to p-tag".

findings.claim: build_add_member and build_remove_member validate the target pubkey with check_hex_len(target_pubkey, 64, ...), which is a MINIMUM-length check (builders.rs:45 `if s.len() < min_len || !s.chars().all(...)`), not an exact-length one. Any hex string of 64 or more characters is accepted and emitted as a `p` tag on a NIP-29 kind:9000/9001 membership event. The file has a correct exact-length validator right beside it — check_pubkey_hex at line 70 (`if s.len() != 64`) — which every other pubkey-taking builder uses; check_hex_len exists for git commit SHAs and even reports the failure as SdkError::InvalidDiffMeta, showing it was copied from the diff-metadata path.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a 128-character hex string (e.g. a signature or a concatenation of two pubkeys) as target_pubkey to build_add_member. Validation passes, and the caller signs a kind:9000 add-member event whose p-tag holds a 128-char value. The relay's membership handler must then be the only thing rejecting it; a builder that is documented as validating its inputs (crates/buzz-sdk/src/lib.rs:11 "Each builder function validates its inputs") has instead signed a structurally invalid membership command, and a truncating consumer that reads the first 64 chars would resolve it to a different pubkey than one reading the last 64.
findings.evidence: check_hex_len(target_pubkey, 64, "target_pubkey")?;

findings.claim: insert_mentions builds one multi-row INSERT with six bind parameters per valid `p` tag and applies no cap on the number of tags, even though the SDK caps the same field at MENTION_CAP = 50 (crates/buzz-sdk/src/mentions.rs:38, enforced in builders.rs:189). The tag list is attacker-chosen and un-deduplicated in Rust (dedup only happens server-side via ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING at lib.rs:165), so the row count and parameter count scale with whatever the relay's frame limit allows.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker publishes a single kind:9 event stuffed with distinct 64-hex `p` tags up to the relay's advertised max_message_length (262,144 bytes per buzz-relay/src/nip11.rs:464), i.e. roughly 3,600-3,900 tags. insert_mentions accepts all of them and issues one INSERT with ~23,000 bind parameters that writes ~3,900 rows into event_mentions, each carrying two indexes (migrations/0001_initial_schema.sql:296-299). Repeating this turns each accepted 256 KiB event into several hundred KiB of indexed mention rows, and every REQ with a `#p` filter (event.rs:371-386) pays for the inflated index. If a deployment raises the frame limit past ~10,900 valid tags the statement exceeds the Postgres 65,535 bind-parameter ceiling and fails outright — and because every call site treats the result as best-effort (`if let Err(e) = insert_mentions(...)` at lib.rs:1626, 2087, 2121, 4562, 4736, 4973) the failure is only logged, leaving the event stored but permanently absent from `#p` filters and the Home Feed.

findings.claim: A NIP-OA agent->owner delegation, once materialized, is permanent: `set_agent_owner` only writes when `agent_owner_pubkey IS NULL`, and no code path anywhere in the workspace ever clears or rotates that column. There is no revocation for an owner attestation once any single request has presented the auth tag, and the relay caches the resulting authority for 5 minutes on the explicit premise that it is immutable (crates/buzz-relay/src/state.rs:603).
findings.failure_scenario: Owner O issues agent key A a NIP-OA auth tag. A (or anyone holding A's tag, since the tag is a bearer credential carried in a plaintext `x-auth-tag` header at crates/buzz-relay/src/api/bridge.rs:803 or a NIP-42 AUTH tag) connects once. crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/auth.rs:258 calls `materialize_nip_oa_owner`, which at crates/buzz-relay/src/api/mod.rs:203 calls `set_agent_owner`, permanently writing `users.agent_owner_pubkey = O` for A in that community. O later wants to revoke: the agent key is compromised, the contractor left, or the tag's own `created_at<` bound has passed. There is no `unset_agent_owner`, no UPDATE ... SET agent_owner_pubkey = NULL, and no admin command in the tree (grep for `agent_owner_pubkey` finds exactly one writer: this line). The mapping continues to authorize O over A's events (NIP-09 deletion at crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/side_effects.rs:250/270 via `is_agent_owner`) and to mark A as O's agent for observer-frame authorization (crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/event.rs:1003), forever. Only direct SQL against the `users` table can undo it.
findings.evidence: r#"UPDATE users SET agent_owner_pubkey = $1 WHERE community_id = $2 AND pubkey = $3 AND agent_owner_pubkey IS NULL"#,

findings.claim: `verify_auth_tag` validates the NIP-OA `conditions` string's *syntax* but never *evaluates* its clauses against anything — it takes no event and has nothing to evaluate against — yet every relay caller treats its `Ok(owner)` return as an unconditional, unexpiring capability. docs/nips/NIP-OA.md:64 states "Verifiers MUST evaluate every clause", and NIP-OA.md:98 names `created_at<...` as the mechanism owners SHOULD use to bound authorization lifetime. In the relay's admission path that bound is a no-op.
findings.failure_scenario: Owner O deliberately scopes a delegation narrowly: `conditions = "kind=1&created_at<1713957000"` (exactly the spec's own test vector at docs/nips/NIP-OA.md:119), intending "this agent may only post text notes, and only until April 2024". Agent A presents that tag as the `x-auth-tag` header or in its NIP-42 AUTH event. `verify_auth_tag` (this function) parses the four elements, calls `validate_conditions` — which only checks the string is well-formed decimal/clause syntax — verifies the Schnorr signature at line 231, and returns `Ok(owner)`. The caller at crates/buzz-relay/src/api/mod.rs:86 immediately maps that to `MembershipDecision::ViaOwner`, granting A the owner's full relay membership for *every* kind and with no expiry check whatsoever; crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/auth.rs:257 then permanently persists the owner relationship. Neither `kind=1` nor the elapsed `created_at<` bound is consulted at any hop. (The CLI does implement clause evaluation — crates/buzz-cli/src/commands/users.rs:196 `auth_conditions_apply` — which confirms the omission is on the relay side, not a spec misreading.)

findings.claim: The deployment-admin plane — the one surface whose DB layer (crates/buzz-db/src/admin_moderation.rs, whose own module doc says it is "the only moderation repository allowed to omit a CommunityId") deliberately bypasses the tenant fence — is authorized solely by comparing the client-supplied `Host` header to a configured string. There is no token, signature, NIP-98 credential, mTLS, or source-IP check in the process, and the router is merged into the same public axum listener as the relay/WebSocket routes (crates/buzz-relay/src/router.rs:60 and :141).
findings.failure_scenario: Operator sets `BUZZ_ADMIN_HOST=admin.example.com` (crates/buzz-relay/src/config.rs:874) and relies on a private ingress, as docs/admin/README.md advises. Any request path that reaches the relay's listener while preserving an attacker-chosen Host — the relay's public IP/port hit directly, a load balancer or service-mesh sidecar that forwards Host verbatim, an SSRF pivot from inside the cluster, or a second ingress class added later — can issue `GET /api/admin/v1/reports` with `Host: admin.example.com` and no Origin header (the Origin check at line 25 only fires when the header is *present*). That returns, unauthenticated, every community's moderation reports across the whole deployment: reporter pubkeys, private reporter notes, full reported message bodies (AdminReportedMessage.content), plus product feedback and its attachment bytes. Honest caveat: docs/admin/README.md explicitly states "The human trust boundary remains the private admin ingress", so this is a deliberate design that pushes authentication entirely to the network layer — the defect is that the application provides zero defence in depth for a cross-tenant read surface co-hosted on the public listener.
findings.evidence: .is_some_and(|host| host == config.host)

findings.claim: `Db::get_api_token_by_hash`, documented one line above as the lookup for an "active (non-revoked) API token", filters on `revoked_at IS NULL` only and never consults `expires_at` — even though it SELECTs that column, and even though the mint path treats `expires_at <= NOW()` as inactive when enforcing the 10-token quota (crates/buzz-db/src/api_token.rs:105). `get_api_token_by_hash_including_revoked` has the same gap.
findings.failure_scenario: A token is minted with `expires_at = now + 24h` via `create_api_token_if_under_limit`. Twenty-five hours later the quota subquery no longer counts it (api_token.rs:105 `AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > NOW())`), so the owner may mint a replacement — but any authenticator that calls `get_api_token_by_hash(community, sha256(presented_token))` and treats a `Some(record)` as success still authenticates the expired token indefinitely. Reachability caveat, stated plainly: I grepped the whole workspace for every `api_tokens` accessor and found no production consumer today — the only non-buzz-db hit is a comment at crates/buzz-relay/src/api/media.rs:206 saying uploads are "independent of bearer-token / api_tokens", and crates/buzz-test-client/tests/conformance_multitenant.rs:572 records that the mint surface "does not exist on the wire". So this is a latent trap in the widest-blast-radius file rather than a live bug: the API is named and documented as the active-token lookup, so the next consumer that wires it up inherits an expiry bypass with nothing in the signature to warn them.

findings.claim: `build_agent_observer_frame`'s guard that the payload is encrypted is a length-range test, not a ciphertext test: `content_looks_like_nip44` (crates/buzz-core/src/observer.rs:53) returns true for *any* string between 132 and 87472 bytes. The builder's error message and doc claim the content "must be NIP-44 v2 ciphertext", but the check cannot distinguish ciphertext from plaintext, and NIP-44 v2 payloads have a trivially checkable shape (base64 of a leading 0x02 version byte, i.e. always beginning `Ag`).
findings.failure_scenario: A caller building an observer telemetry frame (kind 24200 — agent prompts, tool output, and control commands, the most sensitive payloads the agent platform emits) passes a plaintext JSON payload instead of the output of `encrypt_observer_payload`. Any realistic telemetry blob exceeds 132 bytes, so the guard at this line passes, the builder returns an EventBuilder, the caller signs it, and the relay stores and fans out a signed event with cleartext agent telemetry to every subscriber of the `p`-tagged recipient's frames. Neither this gate nor the receiving side's `decrypt_observer_payload` length check would have flagged it at build time. Reported at low confidence on exploitability: every in-repo caller does encrypt first, so this is a missing guardrail on a developer-error path rather than an attacker-reachable one — but it is the only thing standing between a plaintext payload and a signed, broadcast event.

findings.claim: A REQ whose handler task is still running when its WebSocket closes registers a subscription into `sub_registry` and retains a Redis topic that nothing will ever remove, because `remove_connection` (the only reclaim path) already ran. Each such REQ permanently leaks a subscription entry, its fan-out index entries, and one Redis topic refcount.
findings.failure_scenario: Client opens a WS, completes NIP-42 AUTH, sends `["REQ","s",{"kinds":[1]}]`, and immediately closes the socket. `handle_req` was spawned detached at connection.rs:552 and is awaiting `get_accessible_channel_ids_cached` (req.rs:93) — a DB round-trip. Meanwhile `recv_loop` returns, and `handle_active_connection` runs `cancel.cancel()` and awaits only send/heartbeat/auth tasks (connection.rs:260-263), then calls `state.sub_registry.remove_connection(conn.conn_id)` at connection.rs:265 — which finds nothing. The DB call then returns and `handle_req` proceeds to `register_scoped` (req.rs:239) and `retain_topic` (req.rs:252). `remove_connection` is called from exactly one place in the crate (connection.rs:265) and is now past, and `conn_manager.deregister` (connection.rs:271) already ran, so no later code path removes this conn_id. The subscription and its index rows stay in `SubscriptionRegistry` for process lifetime, are scanned on every fan-out for that (community, kind/channel), and `desired_topics` in buzz-pubsub (crates/buzz-pubsub/src/lib.rs:192-208) keeps the Redis SUBSCRIBE alive forever. Repeating REQ-then-close in a loop grows relay memory, fan-out cost, and the Redis subscription set without bound; `buzz_subscriptions_active` also drifts upward permanently.

findings.claim: When a historical-delivery DB query fails mid-REQ, the handler sends EOSE — the NIP-01 "end of stored events" success signal — and returns, silently truncating history instead of reporting the error. Every other error branch in the same function correctly sends CLOSED.
findings.failure_scenario: A client subscribes with two filters, e.g. `["REQ","s",{"#h":"<ch>","kinds":[9],"limit":500},{"#h":"<ch>","kinds":[7]}]`. `query_events_routed` for filter 0 fails (Postgres pool exhaustion, statement timeout, connection reset). The loop at req.rs:320 hits the Err arm, logs a warn, sends EOSE for the subscription and returns — filter 1 is never executed and the already-delivered events from filter 0 (possibly zero) are all the client gets. The client receives a well-formed EOSE and concludes it has the complete stored history, so the UI renders an empty or partial channel with no error and no retry. Compare req.rs:100, :154 and :100's sibling paths, which send `RelayMessage::closed(&sub_id, "error: database error")` for the same class of failure.

findings.claim: A single transient full send buffer during historical delivery aborts the REQ without ever sending EOSE, while the connection stays open and the subscription stays registered — the client waits for an EOSE that will never arrive.
findings.failure_scenario: `conn.send` returns false on the first buffer-full (connection.rs:88-105) but only cancels the connection after `grace_limit` consecutive fulls (default 15, config.rs:519-522). A client on a slow link issues a broad REQ; the relay pushes historical events faster than the socket drains, the 1000-slot data channel (config.rs:508-511, BUZZ_SEND_BUFFER default 1000) fills once, `conn.send` returns false, and `handle_req` returns at req.rs:399 — skipping the `conn.send(RelayMessage::eose(&sub_id))` at req.rs:408. The counter is reset by the next successful send (connection.rs:92), so the socket is not closed and live fan-out for that subscription continues. Most Nostr clients block their "loading history" state until EOSE, so the channel view spins indefinitely even though new events keep arriving. The NIP-50 search lane has the identical shape at req.rs:726-727 returning before the EOSE at req.rs:739.

findings.claim: For kind:9007 (NIP-29 create-group) the channel row is created in the DB at ingest.rs:2497 before imeta validation runs at ingest.rs:2605-2613. An imeta rejection returns an error without running the `pre_created_channel` compensation, which only exists on the event-insert failure path (ingest.rs:2801), leaving an orphaned channel row and a permanently un-retryable create.
findings.failure_scenario: A client (or attacker) submits a signed kind:9007 with `["h","<client-chosen-uuid>"]`, a valid `name` tag, and an `imeta` tag whose `url` points at a blob that does not exist in this tenant's media store. Flow: `create_channel_with_id` succeeds (ingest.rs:2497-2510), `pre_created_channel = Some(client_uuid)` (ingest.rs:2519). kind:9007 is not in `requires_h_channel_scope` (ingest.rs:477-506) so no thread-metadata step intervenes, and it is not kind 0 or 7, so the next reachable failure point is `verify_imeta_blobs` at ingest.rs:2610, which returns `IngestError::Rejected` via `?`. That `?` returns straight out of `ingest_event_inner` — it never reaches the `match ... Err(e) =>` block at ingest.rs:2798 where `soft_delete_channel(tenant.community(), ch_id)` is the compensation. The user sees `OK false "invalid: ..."` ("channel creation failed") but the channel row exists and lists them as owner. Resending the same event returns `accepted: false, "duplicate: channel already exists"` (ingest.rs:2512-2518) forever, so the client's natural retry can never succeed, and each distinct crafted UUID mints another orphan channel row that no event references.

findings.claim: `get_channel` failures are collapsed to `None` with `.ok()`, and the archived-channel gate at ingest.rs:2320-2326 only rejects when the row is `Some(..)` — so a DB error on the channel lookup silently disables the archived check and lets writes land in an archived channel.
findings.failure_scenario: A member of channel C posts a kind:9 stream message with `["h","<C>"]` after C has been archived (archived_at set by the ephemeral-channel reaper or a 9002 archive edit). `state.db.get_channel(...)` transiently fails (pool timeout, connection reset, or the row was hard-deleted) so `.ok()` yields `channel_row = None`. The membership gate still passes because `check_channel_membership` (ingest.rs:515-545) short-circuits on `is_member_cached` returning `Ok(true)` from the in-process cache before it ever needs the row. Control then reaches ingest.rs:2320-2326, whose `if let Some(channel) = &channel_row` body is skipped entirely, so `channel.archived_at.is_some()` is never evaluated and the event is stored into and fanned out from an archived channel. Every other gate in this function that consumes `channel_row` fails closed on `None` (join-request at ingest.rs:2543-2545 rejects, membership re-fetches at ingest.rs:533-538); the archived gate is the sole fail-open consumer. Reachability of the DB-error branch itself is opportunistic rather than attacker-controlled, hence medium rather than high.

findings.claim: The "frame too large" NOTICE is queued on the data channel and then the recv loop breaks, which triggers `cancel.cancel()`; the send loop's biased cancel branch drains only the control channel before emitting Close, so the explanatory NOTICE is racily dropped and the client is disconnected with no reason.
findings.failure_scenario: A client sends a text frame larger than `max_frame_bytes`. recv_loop calls `conn.send(...)` — which is `send_tx.try_send`, the DATA channel (connection.rs:88-89) — then `break`s. Control returns to `handle_active_connection`, which calls `cancel.cancel()` at connection.rs:260. In `send_loop_inner` the `tokio::select!` is `biased` with `cancel.cancelled()` first (connection.rs:324-325); its body drains `ctrl_rx` only (connection.rs:332-336) and then sends `WsMessage::Close(None)` and breaks, so anything still sitting in `data_rx` is discarded. The module's own comment at connection.rs:329-331 states this drain makes "queue frame on ctrl, then cancel" the safe idiom — this call site uses the data channel instead. Whether the NOTICE survives depends on whether the send task happens to be scheduled between the try_send and the cancel, so the failure is intermittent: users on oversized frames sometimes get a bare close with no diagnostic. The same pattern applies to the binary-frame branch at connection.rs:447-452.

findings.claim: `media_upload_rate_limiter` is a `DashMap` keyed by (community, pubkey) that is inserted into on every upload attempt and never swept — no TTL, no eviction, no `retain` anywhere in the crate — so it grows without bound in the number of distinct signing keys seen.
findings.failure_scenario: On a deployment with `BUZZ_REQUIRE_RELAY_MEMBERSHIP` unset (default false, config.rs:532-534), `enforce_relay_membership` at api/media.rs:211-218 admits any valid Blossom signer, so an attacker generates a fresh secp256k1 keypair per request and issues PUT /upload with a valid kind:24242 auth event. Each request reaches `upload_rate_limited` (api/media.rs:88-111) and inserts a new `(CommunityId, [u8;32]) -> (u32, Instant)` entry. The entry survives the request, the 60-second window, and process uptime: grepping the crate shows `media_upload_rate_limiter` is only ever read/inserted at api/media.rs:97 and constructed at state.rs:775, with no eviction call site. Resident memory grows monotonically with the number of distinct keys, eventually OOM-killing the relay pod. `observer_rate_limiter` (state.rs:774, handlers/event.rs:924) has the same no-eviction shape but is gated behind an `is_agent_owner` DB check, so its key space is bounded by registered agents.

let mut entry = state
        .media_upload_rate_limiter
        .entry(key)
        .or_insert((0, now));

findings.claim: The HTTP NIP-98 event-submission path builds its IngestAuth with Scope::all_known() — which includes AdminChannels and AdminUsers — so the ingest scope check for admin-gated kinds is always satisfied for any NIP-98-authenticated relay member submitting over HTTP POST /events. This is a second, independently-reachable instance of the over-grant the breadth pass attributed only to verify_auth_event (NIP-42/WebSocket); the HTTP path never calls verify_auth_event and hard-codes the full scope set here.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who is a relay member (or passes NIP-OA membership) signs a kind:9030/9031/9032 (RELAY_ADMIN_ADD_MEMBER/REMOVE_MEMBER/CHANGE_ROLE) or kind:9000/9001/9005 NIP-29 admin event and POSTs it to /events with a valid NIP-98 Authorization header. In submit_event_authed the auth is built as IngestAuth::Http { scopes: Scope::all_known() }. In ingest.rs, required_scope_for_kind returns Scope::AdminChannels/AdminUsers (line 260/269) and the gate `if !auth.scopes().contains(&required)` (line 1904) passes because all_known() contains both admin scopes. findings.claim: NIP-42 relay-URL normalization aliases `localhost`, `::1`, and `127.0.0.1` into a single host, directly contradicting the sibling NIP-98 verifier which deliberately keeps loopback variants distinct because collapsing them is a documented "host-binding side door" (nip98.rs lines 137-144, with a dedicated test `loopback_aliases_are_distinct_hosts`). Both verifiers are meant to enforce the same conformance row-44 obligation ('AUTH host must match req.community', per bridge.rs lines 208-217), but the WS/NIP-42 side enforces it more weakly than the HTTP/NIP-98 side.
findings.failure_scenario: In a multi-tenant deployment where community A is bound to host `localhost:PORT` and community B to `127.0.0.1:PORT` (plausible in local multi-tenant testing or a loopback misconfiguration), a member of A can present a NIP-42 AUTH event whose `relay` tag is `ws://localhost:PORT` on a WebSocket connection bound to community B; normalize_relay_url rewrites both sides to `ws://127.0.0.1:PORT`, so verify_nip42_event's relay-URL binding passes for the wrong community. The cross-community relay-tag fence that NIP-98 keeps closed is open here. Real production hosts are DNS names (not loopback), so exploitability is confined to loopback-bound tenants — hence low severity / medium confidence.

findings.claim: The primary bridge endpoints /events, /query and /count authenticate via verify_bridge_auth, which calls verify_bridge_auth_with_options with require_payload=false, so a NIP-98 token for these endpoints is not required to carry a `payload` tag and is therefore not cryptographically bound to the request body (verify_nip98_event only checks the SHA-256 body hash when a payload tag is present). This is asymmetric with api/operator.rs and api/invites.rs, which pass require_payload=true. The nip98 module doc itself states the payload tag is what 'prevents body-substitution attacks'.
findings.failure_scenario: On a non-TLS hop (or via any position that can reorder the request), an attacker who observes a victim's NIP-98 Authorization header for POST /query can replay that header with a substituted filter body before the victim's request lands. Because no payload tag was required, verify_nip98_event accepts the swapped body, and because the replay guard marks the event id only on first arrival, the attacker's substituted request wins and returns data scoped to the victim's channel membership while the victim's own request is rejected as replay. The window is the ±60s NIP-98 tolerance and the exploit requires beating the victim in the replay race and a non-TLS/interceptable channel, so this is a defense-in-depth gap — reported at LOW confidence because the reachable path depends on absent TLS and a won race.
findings.evidence: verify_bridge_auth_with_options(headers, method, url, body, require_auth_token, false)

findings.claim: On reconnect the per-subscription replay window's since is derived from lastSeenCreatedAt (the max created_at seen on the live subscription); created_at is sender-chosen (only bounded by the relay's plus/minus 15-minute drift check, and honest clock skew of even a minute exceeds the 5-second RECONNECT_REPLAY_SKEW_SECS tolerance), so a future-dated message pushes since past real time and messages that arrive during a disconnect are never replayed and silently missing.
findings.failure_scenario: A member posts a message with created_at ~10 minutes in the future (accepted: within plus/minus 15-min drift, ingest.rs:1862). Every viewer's live subscription runs prepareSubscriptionEvent (relayClosedRecovery.ts:141) setting lastSeenCreatedAt to that future value. Their socket drops (VPN blip/sleep). On reconnect replaySince = lastSeenCreatedAt - 5s (~10 min future) and buildReconnectReplayFilter sets REQ since to it (relayReconnectReplay.ts:61); the relay returns nothing older than that instant, so real messages posted during the outage (timestamps ~now) fall below since and never arrive — the timeline is missing messages with no error shown.

findings.claim: The reconnect history-paging loop advances pageUntil by at most one second when a full 500-event page shares the oldest created_at, so if more than 500 events share the same one-second timestamp the ones beyond the first page at that second are skipped and never replayed.
findings.failure_scenario: During a >500-event burst within one second (busy channel or agent flood), the relay returns a full 500-event page whose oldest created_at is T. Since events.length === RECONNECT_REPLAY_PAGE_LIMIT the loop continues and pageUntil becomes T-1 (the oldestCreatedAt - 1 branch), excluding every remaining event at exactly T. Those same-second events are dropped from reconnect backfill and only reappear on a manual scrollback.

findings.claim: validate_video_file guards the divisor (timescale==0) before calling mp4::Mp4Track::duration(), but not the dividend. The mp4 crate computes `self.trak.mdia.mdhd.duration * 1_000_000 / timescale` (mp4-0.14.0/src/track.rs:207-210) on a u64 mdhd.duration read verbatim from the attacker's file (mdhd version 1 reads a full u64). Any mdhd.duration above 2^64/10^6 (~1.8e13) overflows the multiply before the division ever happens.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker PUTs /upload with a structurally valid fast-start H.264 MP4 whose mdia/mdhd box is version 1 with duration=0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF and timescale=1000. Entry: buzz-relay/src/api/media.rs:305 upload_blob -> should_stream_as_video (media.rs:49-52, matches the ftyp) -> buzz-media/src/upload.rs:292 process_video_upload -> upload.rs:421 spawn_blocking(validate_video_file) -> validation.rs:293/352. The box shape passes check_moov_before_mdat and validate_mp4_metadata_free (mdhd is in the ALLOWED list at validation.rs:859). In any profile with overflow-checks on (the default dev/test profile; the workspace Cargo.toml sets none) the multiply panics inside spawn_blocking, the JoinError maps to MediaError::Internal (upload.rs:423) and the client gets a 500 with a panic in the logs — a free crash-the-task primitive, repeatable. In release (overflow-checks off) it wraps silently to an arbitrary value, so duration_secs can land under the 600.0 cap at validation.rs:357 and be written into the sidecar as duration_secs (upload.rs:478) and returned as BlobDescriptor.duration — a fabricated duration that buzz-relay/src/handlers/imeta.rs:270 then enforces against the poster's own imeta tag.
